title: How Assefa ran third fastest marathon ever despite 'destroyed' Achilles
text:
Right up until the 40km mark of the Berlin Marathon at the weekend, Tigst Assefa was well on track to regain her world record.

After 10km, the Ethiopian star was already over a minute in the lead of a race that quickly became a challenge between her and the clock.

By the 30km mark, the noted fast-finisher was running inside world record pace and flying.

"She was on [target] to run 2:09:30, 2:09:40," Assefa's representative Gianni Demadonna told The Associated Press on Tuesday.

Tigst Assefa was flying through the first 30km of the race, running well under world record pace. (Getty Images: Maja Hitij)

Official World Marathon Majors social media accounts were excitedly posting "this is on" with Assefa 20 seconds under the existing world record time, set by controversial Kenyan Ruth Chepng'etich.

Chepng'etich's record is 2:09:56 from the 2024 Chicago Marathon, but she hasn't raced since July 2025 after admitting to a doping violation.

She is currently serving a three-year ban. There is no suggestion that Chepng'etich doped in Chicago and that record still stands.

Assefa was within touching distance of eliminating Chepng'etich from the record books.

But, within sight of the Brandenburg Gate at just 2 kilometres remaining, Assefa began to grimace, then started to limp and hobbled to the line.

She eventually finished 68 seconds shy of Chepng'etich's record.

Assefa suffered 'complete rupture of the right Achilles tendon'

Assifa's finishing time of 2:11:04 was the third-fastest in history and gave the Olympic silver medallist her third career victory in Berlin, in a new course record.

But incredibly, it was later revealed that the 29-year-old had suffered a "complete rupture of the right Achilles tendon" and has since undergone surgery.

According to her team, Assefa had felt pain in her Achilles from the 31st kilometre, but pushed on regardless, before complete disaster struck with just 2km to go.

Tigst Assefa was unable to stand after crossing the line. (Getty Images: picture alliance/Andreas Gora)

The Achilles tendon connects your calf muscles to your heel bone and lifts the heel when the calf muscle contracts.

"Your Achilles is basically a spring to propel yourself forward," Zoe Russell, a specialist sports and exercise physio as awarded by the Australian College of Physiotherapists, told ABC Sport.

"It transfers your load to propel you forward.

"Tendon experts around the world sort of suggest that a painful tendon doesn't often rupture because it just can't sustain the load.

"You don't typically hear this story of how they're running along, they're sore and then it pops."

How can you run with a ruptured Achilles?

Associate Professor Peter Malliaras, a physiotherapist and clinical researcher at Monash University, told ABC Radio National's Health Report in 2022 that an Achilles tendon rupture "is quite a catastrophic injury".

"It will prevent you from pretty much doing everything in your daily functions; including walking, running, driving, for a fair period of time," he said.

Tigst Assefa could barely struggle to her feet. (Getty Images: Anadolu/Halil Sagirkaya)

Demadonna claimed that Assefa "completely destroyed the tendon" by the end of the race, running the final 500 metres without it.

"She was no longer able to run, because when she was going to put her foot on the ground she had no power," Demadonna said.

Adidas one-run-and-done shoe sets new mark in sport's arms race Adidas's new running shoe helped Ethiopia's Tigst Assefa take more than 2 minutes off the marathon world record in Berlin at the weekend — but if you want to get hold of the one-run-and-done shoe, you'd better start saving.

Yet Assefa was still able to finish the race, running along at a fair lick too, despite being unable to push off with her forefoot.

One reason for her ability to keep moving forward could be found in the super shoes she was wearing, with the integrated carbon plate essentially providing some of the spring instead.

"It could have helped her keep going, yes," Russell suggested.

"Those carbon plates will allow you to transfer your load a bit easier."

Nevertheless, Assefa collapsed soon after crossing the line in clear distress before support arrived, including Ethiopian long-distance running legend Haile Gebrselassie.

Quick surgery vital

She was immediately flown to Munich by private jet courtesy of her sponsor, Adidas, where Demadonna said she underwent "very complex surgery" on Monday.

Without knowing the exact details of the rupture, or the exact surgery technique used, Russell said a time frame for a return would be impossible to guess, but noted that quick surgery was essential.

"Things can move quickly, really quickly in elite sport," she said.

"I've had athletes get an appointment with a surgeon within 20 minutes, half an hour of the injury.

Tigst Assefa was aided by four-time Berlin winner Haile Gebrselassie to leave the finishing area. (Getty Images: Maja Hitij)

"When you've got means and connections at the elite level, things can move very quickly — and you do want to move fairly quickly with an Achilles rupture because it is constantly under tension. When it ruptures, it actually retracts back.

"So if you're waiting weeks for surgery, it means that your muscles actually start to suffer the effects of de-conditioning and it retracts, which makes for a technically harder surgical process because you've got to pull it and put it all on tension and then stitch it up.

"For an elite athlete, you'd want to get it in two or three days, whereas in the general population, you'll probably get away with getting it within a week."

In a statement, Assefa's coach Gemedu Dedifo said that she "successfully underwent surgery" within 24 hours.

"Tigst is a champion," the statement read.

"We believe in her strength, courage and determination.

"We look forward to seeing her recover and return to the track and roads."

Assefa vows to return

Assefa sent a message from her hospital bed via the Berlin Marathon organisers, defiantly promising to return to break the record.

"My surgery went well," she said in a statement.

"I am overwhelmed by the tremendous support I have received from all over the world. From the bottom of my heart, I would like to thank everyone for their incredible support and concern.

"I will definitely come back to Berlin, and then I will break the world record."

Tigst Assefa holds the women's only world record. (Getty Images: Xinhua/Li Ying)

No marathon has seen more world records than Berlin, with 13 set at the race since 1974 thanks to its largely flat profile with just 73 metres of elevation gain and 79 metres of elevation loss over the 42km.

Assefa set one of those world records in 2023, running 2:11:53 to become the first woman to set a record on the course since Sydney Olympic champion Naoko Takahashi did so in 2001.

Assefa already holds the women's only world record, having run 2:15:41 to win the 2026 London Marathon in April.

Races where men and women start at the same time, as is the case in Berlin, tend to be faster for women, who are able to benefit from male pacemakers who can block the wind and reduce fatigue earlier in the race.

title: Dairy farm flooded, but grain growers rejoice as Victoria settles in for wet weekend
text:
Soaking rain continues to fall across parts of Victoria, after storms caused tree falls, power outages, building damage and six rescues.

State Emergency Service (SES) state duty officer Shane McBride said crews had received 200 calls for help since midday yesterday.

"It's been a very hectic last 24 hours.

"But the number that's really scary at the moment is six flood rescues we've had," he said.

VICSES said it would improve its payroll processes to avoid future problems. (ABC News: Kathy Lord)

Mr McBride said flash flooding could develop quickly and urged people not to drive through floodwater.

"It's best just to avoid it at all costs."

Minor flooding on a street in Sale, central Gippsland. (ABC News: Jack Colantuono)

Gippsland dairy farms flooded

Dairy farmer Nicole Saunders said her Maffra farm was already under water with much more rain yet to fall.

"The amount of rain we've already had overnight … everything is already really saturated and it's not even the biggest [rainfall] yet," Ms Saunders said.

The Berry Dairy owner Nicole Saunders has decided to close the business for several days due to the impact of the heavy rainfall. (Supplied: The Berry Dairy)

More than 100 millimetres of rain is forecast for parts of Gippsland into tomorrow.

Ms Saunders milks 600 dairy cows and runs a strawberry farm and said she had spent much of the past day moving stock to higher ground.

"After three days of rain, Sunday is possibly when it's going to be peak flooding," Ms Saunders said.

She said the October 2023 floods taught her that water could move across the flood plain in unexpected ways.

"There's lots of areas where the water will just cascade across," Ms Saunders said.

Slow-moving low pressure system

Bureau of Meteorology meteorologist Ursula Connor said a slow-moving low pressure system was expected to drift east tomorrow, with showers and thunderstorms continuing across central and eastern Victoria.

"We're expected to see a very persistent and gusty south-easterly flow picking up through tomorrow," Ms Connor said.

"This is going to drive a lot of moisture into southern parts of the state and we see the risk of heavy to maybe even locally intense rainfall developing from the early hours of tomorrow morning, particularly over the Otways and the Strzelecki Ranges," she said.

Murtoa farmer John Delahunty says the rain is just enough at exactly the right time. (Supplied)

Dream season for farmers

While the persistent rain could cause riverine and flash flooding in eastern Victoria, grain growers in the state's west said their spring drop was just enough to set the season up perfectly.

John Delahunty farms at Murtoa in the Wimmera and said it had been a season that just kept delivering rain at the right times.

"Rain hasn't been our limiting factor this year, it's really just been a beautiful season really," he said.

"All the crops are starting fill now and the rain last night and today, from a farmer's perspective, it's brilliant."

Martin Colbert says the spring rain has set the season up for "record potential yields". (Supplied)

Agriculture consultant Martin Colbert, also based in the Wimmera, said the rain over the past 24 hours was the second most important of the season, after the opening rains in autumn.

"The season had allowed crops to set record potential yields and the only outstanding obstacle was a final rain to ensure grain fill," he said.

"That is exactly where the crops will be when this rain event has passed; legumes and oil seeds are podding and cereals are either flowering or filling."

Powercor said 3,000 customers in the Heathcote area were without power during storms last night.

title: Roosters blow as Watson ruled out
text:
The Sydney Roosters have suffered a significant blow ahead of the NRL grand final, with hooker Connor Watson ruled out of the match.

In a cruel blow, Watson will miss Sunday's decider against his former club Newcastle and become the first player to sit out a grand final as a result of a concussion.

Watson was dazed and was taken from the field moments after coming on in the Roosters' preliminary final win over the Dolphins.

Under the NRL's protocol, players diagnosed with a category-one concussion, as Watson was, face a mandatory stand-down period of 11 days.

The Roosters had indicated that Watson was testing well leading into Thursday when the 30-year-old met with an independent specialist.

But on Friday the club confirmed the utility had failed to receive clearance to line up in the grand final.

The outcome means Watson has played his last game for the Roosters with the popular utility heading to St George Illawarra next season before linking up with the PNG Chiefs in 2028.

Connor Watson has played 127 games for the Roosters in the NRL. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Watson's absence likely forces Roosters coach Trent Robinson's hand when it comes to his bench, with hooker Benaiah Ioelu the most obvious man to come into Easts' 19-man squad.

Ioelu has played mostly off the bench through his 17-game NRL career, starting just once in five appearances this season, and would act as cover for Reece Robson.

"I don't think it takes too much to work out what plan B is, but we have got some really good hookers," Robinson said on Thursday.

"Benaiah Ioelu played some great footy for us this year. He brings a lot of energy to us as well so he will come into consideration then."

Newcastle, meanwhile, are also expected to face a tough decision leading into Sunday's decider as they weigh up a replacement for suspended number nine, Phoenix Crossland.

Harrison Graham has excelled as a bench option at hooker for the Knights, but coach Justin Holbrook, who doesn't have to name his final team until 90 minutes before kick-off on Sunday, has the option of also starting Thomas Cant or Diesel Hagan.

ABC/AAP

title: Greene joins Cats as AFL teams make off-season moves
text:
Toby Greene has become the first major AFL free agency domino to fall, with Greater Western Sydney to receive a second-round draft pick for losing their former captain to Geelong.

The Cats lodged paperwork on Friday to land the inaugural Giant as an unrestricted free agent.

Greene, a triple All Australian and dual club champion, booted 450 goals across his 15-year, 282-game tenure for GWS.

The 33-year-old cited family reasons for returning to his native Victoria and reuniting with his close mate and former Giants forward Jeremy Cameron at the Cattery on a lucrative three-year deal.

The Giants will receive a second-round draft selection as compensation, currently slated at number 26.

Earlier, key forward Joel Amartey's switch from Sydney to Carlton was confirmed as the free agency period opened.

The Swans will receive draft compensation for losing the unrestricted 27-year-old, who was an emergency during finals after failing to convince coach Dean Cox following a partial Achilles tear.

Paperwork will be lodged later on Friday to rubber-stamp Lachie Neale's move to Collingwood as an unrestricted free agent after the Brisbane Lions star added a third premiership medal to his swag of silverware.

Melbourne's 2021 premiership vice-captain Jack Viney is poised for a move with two years remaining on his contract after meeting with West Coast.

After being sidelined through injury for all but one game this season, the 32-year-old was told by coach Steven King there would likely be limited opportunities for him in the Demons midfield.

"Footy's gone that way mate," Viney told 10 News at Perth Airport on Thursday.

"So took a bit to process early days, but we're here now, so we'll make the best of the opportunity … it [a deal] will get done."

Neale set to join Magpies Collingwood says it "looks forward" to Lachie Neale joining the club in 2027 after it is announced he is leaving the Brisbane Lions.

Young Hawthorn forward Calsher Dear, meanwhile, has opted to stay at the Hawks on a two-year deal after weighing up a potential move to the Dees.

The 21-year-old, son of late 1991 Norm Smith medallist Paul Dear, burst onto the scene in his debut season with 25 goals from 17 appearances in 2024.

But the emerging tall has struggled to hold his spot through injury and internal competition, adding just 14 games in 2025 and 2026.

"We are very excited about what the future holds for Calsher with a strong pre-season under his belt and greater continuity into 2027 and beyond," Hawks list manager Mark McKenzie said.

Hawthorn's key forward selection squeeze is set to worsen in 2027, with Gold Coast's restricted free agent Ben King expected to join Jack Gunston, Mitch Lewis, Mabior Chol and Dear.

AAP

title: Qld government takes data centre approvals from councils to avoid 'inconsistency'
text:
The Queensland government will take the planning and assessment of data centre applications away from local councils under a new system.

It comes as Australia's largest proposed data centre is planned for the Western Downs, 200 kilometres west of Brisbane, in an area rich in agriculture and coal seam gas wells.

The state government said the new planning framework would mirror its changes to renewable energy developments by requiring a social impact assessment and a community benefit agreement to be made with the local council before a development application was lodged.

The concept model of a large-scale data centre project that has been proposed for the Western Downs. (Supplied: Urbis)

Developers are increasingly eyeing sites across Queensland as locations for data centres to power artificial intelligence development due to the state's available land and capacity to connect to the energy grid.

Queensland is also yet to put in place dedicated planning for data centre infrastructure, unlike Victoria and New South Wales.

The state government said the changes would ensure a "consistent and transparent framework across the state".

"Many councils don't include data centres in their planning schemes, which creates confusion and inconsistency," the state government said in a statement.

"We will treat these projects no worse and no better than we do mining, renewables or tourism projects," it said.

"Any deals must be done with the backing of councils and communities."

'Non-negotiables' for Queensland

Premier David Crisafulli said data centre investment would need to create local jobs and drive down electricity bills.

"If data centres want to do business in Queensland, here's the non-negotiables: you're not going in people's backyards, you're not pinching our power, and you're not shipping our data off overseas," Mr Crisafulli said on Thursday.

"And if all of those can be done, and if the investment can be in driving down people's power bills and we create some jobs in the process, big tick."

About 46 per cent of the nation's feedlot occupancy is located within 200 kilometres of Dalby, according to the Western Downs Regional Council. (ABC Rural: Brandon Long)

Council 'guaranteed' to retain control

Despite the planned changes, Western Downs Mayor Andrew Smith said he had been given assurances from the state government that his council would remain the assessment manager for the Western Downs proposal.

"We're not surprised they're introducing a new planning framework," he said.

"But we have been assured we will remain the assessment manager for the Western Downs Digital Park."

Cr Smith said he remained confident in the council's ability to make an informed and appropriate decision.

"We will control what we can control. We will stick to the facts as assessment managers," he said.

International developer Zerra DC lodged plans for the hyper-scale computing project in August. Anthropic, the company behind artificial intelligence assistant Claude, has since signed on to lease the first of four planned buildings at the site.

While the Western Downs Regional Council says it has no firm timeframe for assessing the application, the developer wants the state government to step in to speed up the approvals process.

Zerra DC has applied for "prescribed process" status under state government rules, which would allow Queensland's coordinator-general to take over the decision-making from the council.

title: 'Snowball effect' hitting as companies react to rates rise, growing costs
text:
Nick and Amanda Kuhn run an organic egg business in the rural town of Tiaro, about 220 kilometres north of Brisbane.

The pair say their family-run operation has been struggling to slow the "snowball effect" of rising costs.

"There comes a point where you just can't keep wearing the cost because you're wearing so much but you can't keep charging more for your product," Mr Kuhn said.

"It's a very fine balancing act."

A recent report from Business Chamber Queensland found confidence in the economy was at its lowest level since the Global Financial Crisis.

It found 95 per cent of businesses were feeling an impact of higher fuel prices, with at least 60 per cent reporting higher costs from freight, transport and cashflow issues.

'Less profit for the business'

The Reserve Bank lifted the cash rate for the fourth time this year on Wednesday, pushing rates to their highest level since 2011, at 4.6 per cent.

Mr Kuhn said his home mortgage repayments increased by "roughly $1,000 a month", due to the hikes.

"It's harder to service loans. It's harder to get new loans if you want equipment or other things," he said.

Businesses have now been banned from adding a surcharge to card payments, which Mr Kuhn said helped cover expenses including petrol and wages.

"It's going to cost us a couple of thousand dollars to wear that, it's less profit for the business," he said.

To recoup any losses, Mr Kuhn told customers there would be a price hike on egg cartons.

Christopher Hall has been forced to raise the price of his honey products for the first time in a decade to stay afloat. (Supplied: Christopher Hall)

Hervey Bay honey producer Christopher Hall was also grappling with whether to increase the price of his raw honey buckets to $16 per kilogram.

"In the previous 10 years we've just absorbed the increased costs because it's important to maintain honey as cheap as I possibly can," Mr Hall said.

"We simply can't do that anymore."

Mr Hall said the extra revenue would cover rising petrol prices and growing cost of plastic containers, which is up by nearly 40 per cent this year.

Tough times ahead

CQ University regional economics development professor John Rolfe said it could take up to 18 months for this week's interest rate hike to "wash through the system".

Professor Rolfe said businesses needed to make calculated spending decisions to ensure they can survive.

"Be prepared to make an early call about cutting costs so they don't get caught out," he said.

Professor John Rolfe says it could take 18 months for the interest rate rises to "wash through the system". (Supplied: CQ University)

But Professor Rolfe said not to expect relief any time soon.

"Governments are under pressure to not spend as much to try and get inflation down," he said.

Despite the struggles, Mr Hall said he and his business will endure.

"We have had to increase prices to stay afloat but small producers do make the world go round," he said.

title: NRLW grand final marks end of era
text:
One year after the greatest and most controversial grand final in the NRLW, we're right back where we were 12 months ago.

Once again the Roosters will face Brisbane, with the Broncos all that stands between the Tricolours and a perfect season.

But while the season seems to be ending in the same place, the changes in the two sides, plus those that loom in the near future, make this game feel like the end of an era.

Controversial try decides NRLW premiership Brisbane and the Roosters played one of the greatest games in NRLW history, but the controversial winning try to Mele Hufanga shapes as a football mystery that might never be solved.

Roosters Millie Elliott and Corban Baxter will retire after the match, while New South Wales Origin prop Rima Butler is bound for Wests Tigers.

But where they limped into the decider last year, without injured halfback Tarryn Aiken and winger Taina Naividi after she broke down at the club's final training session, this time they're fully loaded.

The Broncos have not quite been the dominant force they were last year but they showed their class downing the Gold Coast in last week's preliminary final and have extra motivation of their own.

Ali Brigginshaw, one of the icons of the NRLW's early years, will be playing her last game before hanging up the boots.

Throw in lingering feelings from last year's 22-18 Broncos victory, which was sealed by a contentious try to Brisbane centre Mele Hufanga with three minutes left, and the stakes could not be higher.

The Roosters are determined to run towards the bad memories, having watched a replay of the match together before the season began.

"We're building on the feelings from last year," five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher said.

"It was a big theme of our pre-season camp.

"We watched it all together and it was really hard. There were a lot of people getting emotional but it was dead silent. It was so eerie.

"We all feel the hurt and the pain from last year. We won't let it happen again. We've worked so hard to fix those little things that went wrong last year."

After another undefeated regular season, that grand final loss is the only time the Roosters have had their colours lowered in the past two years, giving them 30 wins from their last 31 starts.

The Roosters have humbled their opponents this year. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

It meant they'd forgotten what defeat could even feel like. While they'll keep talk about it to a minimum this week, there's no doubt it hangs over them like a spectre.

"At the time, it was a weird feeling because the result was disappointing, but there was a lot of things in the lead-up that didn't go our way," hooker Keeley Nizza said.

"That's rugby league though and we still had the opportunity to win it but we didn't. The way we rallied together and played well regardless of the result, it brought us closer together.

"We won't speak about it too much, so it won't need to be brought up. It's always with us. Every year there's a new squad and a new feel, but we won't forget."

That possibility of a new squad in 2027 is why the match feels like the end of something.

Elliott is a Test and Origin mainstay, Baxter has played for the club since 2019, Butler has blossomed since joining Newcastle, and each of them leaves a serious hole in the roster with their departure.

Millie Boyle is one of three key players appearing in their last game for the Roosters. (Getty Images: Matt King)

The Roosters have done an excellent job identifying and progressing talent through their women's program, but all three are exceptionally difficult to replace.

While the club will be a premiership threat for some years to come, this game could mark the end of the club as a historically dominant force.

The combined impact of the departing trio makes them just a little more like everyone else, which could make this their last chance at the elusive perfect season.

Brisbane have already felt the pinch hurting the Roosters now. They have eight changes from last year's grand final, including Hufanga, who left for the Warriors.

But they did welcome in Blues halfback Jesse Southwell, and with her and Brigginshaw calling the shots, the Broncos attack is sure to fire.

Plus the defending premiers boast newly minted three-time Dally M and two-time Karyn Murphy Medal winner Tamika Upton, who's won three of the past four premierships across two different clubs.

Brigginshaw's last 'last' in NRLW grand final Ali Brigginshaw and fellow OGs Julia Robinson and Chelsea Lenarduzzi are hoping to join Broncos royalty with a fifth NRLW premiership.

Given her record in big matches, she's sure to put her stamp on the game and is good enough to win it almost on her own, meaning the result is well and truly up for grabs.

The Roosters were in imperious form to end the regular season, winning their last four regular season games by a combined total of 200 points to 34, but any thought of catching them complacent was ended in the preliminary final against Canberra.

The gallant Raiders gave a fine account of themselves in an intensely physical encounter, and the 20-10 Roosters win has them primed to hit their straps when it matters most.

"That's the sorest I've felt all year," Kelleher said.

"We absolutely bashed each other up on that field for 70 full minutes."

"We showed our mindset, that we could go through the grit and the arm wrestle. It's the perfect lead in to a grand final."

title: Piastri likens track to 'sandpaper' as F1 returns to Malaysia
text:
Formula 1 is heading back to Malaysia's Sepang International Circuit after a nine-year hiatus this weekend, with more than half the drivers on the grid unfamiliar with a track that is hosting the rescheduled Bahrain Grand Prix.

After making its first appearance on the calendar in 1999, Sepang has not hosted a Formula 1 race since 2017 after the Malaysian government said it could no longer justify the costs given the declining returns.

But it is making its F1 comeback after owners Liberty Media said it would host the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, relocating the race from Sakhir due to the Iran war and the situation in the Middle East.

Russell wins Azerbaijan GP after Piastri disaster in Baku George Russell has claimed a nail-biting victory in Baku, holding off Max Verstappen by just 0.196 seconds to secure his third victory of the season.

The 5.543-km long circuit combines long straights with several high-speed corners, with this week's race set to be held over 56 laps.

Only 10 of the 22 drivers have previously raced in Malaysia, leaving world champion Lando Norris and his McLaren teammate Oscar Piastri among those who will be learning the track for the first time.

Tyre supplier Pirelli has warned teams to expect challenging conditions, describing Sepang's surface as "relatively abrasive" with roughness comparable to Bahrain.

Piastri said the track "looks like sandpaper" and he too expected a lot of tyre degradation.

"I don't know how much racing or track running there's been recently. And anything that has been, the rain probably washes it off every afternoon anyway," Piastri said.

"So it's going to be a pretty tough weekend for everyone."

Thunderstorms are far from unusual in Malaysia, where the tropical climate regularly produces heavy afternoon showers and lightning storms.

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli said Sepang's notorious abrasive surface could prove a welcome surprise should F1 finally get its first wet race of the season in Malaysia.

The young Italian, who has enjoyed a charmed run of dry conditions throughout his title charge, reckons the Malaysian circuit's rough tarmac would make it the ideal venue to test the sport's 2026 cars in challenging weather.

"I think this track will be quite OK in the wet … The surface is so open, there's actually not a lot of standing water unless it pours down," Antonelli told reporters, adding that it was the "roughest track tarmac" he had ever seen.

"But if it rains normally, then it would probably be the best track to try these cars for the first time in the rain because the tarmac is so open that the water just doesn't sit on top of the surface. It actually goes in between the stones. So it makes less risk of aquaplaning."

Reuters

title: Which states get a public holiday on Monday?
text:
Many Australians are set to enjoy a three-day weekend, with half the country having a public holiday on Monday.

But other Australians will have to wait at least a month until their next public holiday.

Here's a state-by-state breakdown of the public holidays coming up.

Who gets a public holiday on Monday?

ACT

New South Wales

Queensland

South Australia

The ACT, New South Wales and South Australia have a public holiday for Labour Day.

But in Queensland, Monday is the King's Birthday public holiday.

The Northern Territory, Tasmania, Victoria and Western Australia do not have a public holiday on Monday.

Not everyone have a public holiday on Monday. (ABC News: Kylie Silvester)

What is Labour Day?

It's not a celebration of the political party, but a commemoration of the labour movement, which advocated for rights for workers.

A key date for the movement in Australia was April 21, 1856, when a group of stonemasons in Melbourne protested, demanding an eight-hour workday.

"It was the first of a long, hard-fought series of victories that led to Australia having one of the most progressive labour environments in the world by the early 20th century," the National Museum Australia says.

While this first march led to a victory for some workers in the construction industry, other workers generally worked longer hours and received less pay.

New South Wales and Victoria eventually passed the Eight Hours Act in 1916.

But it wasn't until 1948 that a national 40-hour, five-day working week was approved by the Commonwealth Arbitration Court.

Countries around the world have public holidays commemorating the workers' rights movement, with alternative names like International Workers' Day or May Day.

Workers' unions often hold marches, using the day to continue to advocate for members.

Union members march with banners through Brisbane on Queensland's Labour Day in 2019. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

The public holiday is marked on different days depending on where you live in Australia.

Western Australia's Labour Day public holiday was on March 2 this year.

Victoria and Tasmania marked the day a week later on March 9; however, it's called Eight Hours Day in Tasmania.

The Northern Territory and Queensland observed the public holiday on May 4 this year; however, it's called May Day in the Northern Territory.

When is King Charles's actual birthday?

King Charles III was born on November 14.

But many Commonwealth countries designate a day in June to mark the sovereign's birthday.

This doesn't have anything to do with his predecessor — the late Queen Elizabeth II, whose birthday is on April 21.

It comes from the tradition of holding a military parade to honour the sovereign, with weather in the UK generally more favourable for outdoor events in June.

While June is one of the colder months in Australia, it's generally much sunnier in the Northern Hemisphere at that time of the year.

British royals gather at Buckingham Palace in July each year for a military parade, which began as a way to honour the reigning monarch. (AP Photo: Kirsty Wigglesworth)

Most Australian states had the King's Birthday public holiday on June 8 this year, with the exception of Queensland and Western Australia.

While most of Western Australia had the public holiday on September 28, the Karratha and Port Hedland local government districts designated the holiday for August 3.

When is the next public holiday?

After this weekend, there aren't too many public holidays left in the year.

Sources: Fair Work Ombudsman; Business Victoria; and WorkSafe Tasmania

When does daylight saving time start?

This weekend also marks the start of daylight saving time, but only in some parts of the country.

On Sunday morning, daylight saving time begins in the following jurisdictions:

ACT

New South Wales

South Australia

Tasmania

Victoria

Clocks will move forward by one hour.

title: A classic coming-of-age novel spurred this writer to 'blow up' her life
text:
When Grace Chapple visited Florence, Italy, in 2022, she was listening to the audiobook of A Room with a View.

Travelling solo for the first time, aged 27, she found herself in the Uffizi Gallery — where Botticelli's The Birth of Venus hangs — feeling unsure what to do with her life.

"I was thinking, 'Do I even know who I am?'" Chapple says.

"You know that first time you're forced to confront yourself alone and how you interact with the world?"

As she wandered the city, a little hungover, so too did the protagonist of the novel: Lucy Honeychurch.

In English author EM Forster's 1908 novel A Room with a View, Lucy visits Italy, chaperoned by her spinster cousin Charlotte Bartlett.

There, she meets the charismatic but strange George Emerson and is wooed by another suitor, the wealthy but condescending Cecil Vyse.

It's the set-up for a love triangle, but Forster's novel was more than a romance; it's Lucy's coming-of-age story, which also pokes fun at turn-of-the-century English society.

That complexity spurred Chapple to adapt it for Sydney's Belvoir St Theatre, where it opens this month before travelling to Melbourne Theatre Company.

" The novel hit me hard," she says. "It found me at the moment in my life where I really needed it. "

Listening to A Room with a View in Florence did more than inspire Chapple creatively. It encouraged her to "blow up" her life.

Returning to Sydney, where she had moved from Perth to study playwriting at the National Institute of Dramatic Art (NIDA), Chapple broke up with her long-term boyfriend.

"When you're stuck on train tracks in life, you need something huge to shake you out of it," Chapple says.

Finding inspiration at home

That year, Chapple's debut play, Never Closer, set during the Troubles, premiered as part of Belvoir's independent 25A program. Two years later, it opened on the theatre's main stage.

Grace Chapple was working front-of-house at Belvoir when Never Closer premiered in 2022. (Supplied: Belvoir/Brett Boardman)

A new production from indie company Patalog Theatre will return to Melbourne this month, after earning rave reviews in May.

Never Closer is the story of five schoolfriends reuniting for Christmas Eve at Deidre's house in Northern Ireland in 1987.

Seeing each other a decade after they finished school, with many of them leaving Northern Ireland to work and study, unresolved tensions rise to the surface, especially after Niamh brings home her English fiancé Harry.

It was the play Chapple wrote while studying at NIDA.

She recalls being asked when she applied: "If you had a year left to live, what would you write about?"

She doesn't know why she burst into tears: "I just said, 'My mum'."

Chapple's mum grew up in Northern Ireland and moved to London at 17 to study medicine, where she met Chapple's dad, an Englishman.

"That became the base of the play," Chapple explains.

Chapple's mum loved Never Closer and was inspired to start writing too. (Supplied: Theatre company/Photographer)

"But it was mixed in with the fact I had just left home for the first time and was dealing with all these weird feelings about leaving behind my friends and my home and not knowing if there would be a home to go back to.

" It made me think about my mum and how she never went back. "

Beneath the period romance

After members of the Belvoir team saw Never Closer during its 25A season, they wanted to know what Chapple was going to do next.

"They were keen to invest in me as an artist," she says.

"They said, 'What else do you have? Is there anything you want to adapt you might be able to turn around quicker than an original?'"

When she listened to A Room with a View earlier that year, Chapple had been struck by its theatricality.

" [Forster] writes in scenes and it's all about relationships," she explains. "The action hinges around conversations. "

With buy-in from Never Closer director Hannah Goodwin, Chapple pitched the adaptation to Belvoir artistic director Eamon Flack.

"At first glance it feels like a quite conventional period romance … but the romance is really a vehicle for talking about more exciting political and transgressive topics than we're used to getting out of your Jane Austens," she explains.

Nathalie Morris (Bump) stars as Lucy in Grace Chapple's adaptation of A Room with a View. (Supplied: Belvoir/Brett Boardman)

Chapple says A Room with a View resonates with a modern audience because Lucy is, like all young people, "learning to think for yourself in a world that is really trying to tell you how to think".

"It's about how dangerous it can be to a dominant culture when people start to break away and carve their own paths.

"It's a journey everyone has to go on of figuring out how to live honestly in this world and be true to the person you are and how much that can cost."

A show about the housing crisis

That question of cost is something Chapple is thinking about with her next project, her second original play, The Landlord, which will feature in Belvoir's 2027 season.

It reunites the writer with Goodwin and Never Closer star Ariadne Sgouros (High Country) and breaks down intergenerational inequality in a story set across two Surry Hill terraces. Both are owned by 65-year-old John — but only one is falling apart.

Chapple started writing The Landlord in 2024, when she was on a research trip to Cambridge University to pore over its archive of Forster's manuscripts and diaries for her A Room with a View.

Eamon Flack describes Grace Chapple's The Landlord, starring Ariadne Sgouros, as "cut-glass sharp". (Supplied: Belvoir/Daniel Boud)

"[The Landlord] is born out of just all the dehumanising experiences that come from being a renter," she says.

It's a subject many millennial artists are grappling with in their work.

"Every conversation I've had since I moved to Sydney works its way back to the housing crisis eventually," Chapple says.

"Like, someone's got a shitty rental situation or they're getting kicked out or they're paying too much or they're trying to buy and can't."

While it's the subject on everyone's lips, not everyone has Chapple's expertise.

She's approaching the subject armed with a degree in economics.

"I was taught the narratives that are constructed around capitalism that protect it and make it seem like this perfect, inevitable thing," she says.

"I liked the idea of unpicking the narratives I was taught, but for people who didn't study it."

A Room with a View is at Belvoir St Theatre, Sydney, from October 3 - November 1 and Melbourne Theatre Company from November 14 - December 19.

Never Closer is at fortyfivedownstairs, Melbourne, from October 15 - November 1.

The Landlord is at Belvoir St Theatre, Sydney, from September 25 - October 24, 2027.

title: This public hospital has a 'dazzling' cancer technology and it's not where you think
text:
A "dazzling" new cancer technology that can halve radiation therapy treatments is now available for the first time to public hospital patients, but they will need to be in western NSW to receive it.

The Western Cancer Clinic in Dubbo is the first public hospital in Australia that offers a more dynamic and precise form of radiation therapy called RapidArc Dynamic (RAD).

More than 110 patients have been treated using RAD at the Western Cancer Centre so far.

University of NSW Professor of Radiation Oncology Geoff Delaney said RAD could slash the number of radiation treatments needed and halve the time patients spend being treated in hospital.

He said having the technology in Dubbo was a win for rural patients.

"There's lots of stories where country patients don't get the latest technology, and this is the reverse of that," he said.

Faster treatment

RAD uses a device called a collimator, which shapes the radiation beam to match the exact shape of the cancerous tumour.

It rotates around the patient as the beams are adjusted in real time.

RAD is a step up from RapidArc because it can pause at any point during treatment and deliver more precise dosing.

Acting chief radiation therapist for the Western NSW Local Health District, Catherine Osborne, said the precise dosage protects surrounding organs in cases like breast cancer.

"We're treating all breast tissue, but we don't want to give a radiation dose to the heart and lung, which cause long-term toxicities," she said.

Dr Osborne says radiation technology is continuously evolving and becoming more efficient. (ABC Western Plains: Lily Plass )

Dr Osbourne said medical centres across Australia were "moving very quickly to get RAD", but Dubbo was the first public hospital to do so.

"We have capacity to make our own strategic decision of what technologies we invest in and how we see benefits to our patients," she said.

"So this has really been driven from within."

Dr Osborne said spending even a few minutes less on the treatment bed could make a big difference for patients.

"The difference between three or four minutes and seven or eight minutes is a long time when you're on a hard bed every day, day after day and you're having to do things like fill your bladder or hold your breath," she said.

Big relief for patients

For patients who travel hundreds of kilometres for cancer treatments in Dubbo, having to spend less time in hospital is a relief.

After receiving a brain tumour diagnosis last year, Kevin Barrington from Coonabarabran was one of the first patients to access RAD.

RAD limits radiation to healthy organs. (ABC Western Plains: Lily Plass )

The 78-year-old's treatment time took seven weeks but did not require as much time on the table.

"Whereas it was a sort of half an hour thing a little while ago, I was in and out in about 15 minutes," he said.

" As a layman, it's just dazzling technology. "

Learning with the best

The state-of-the-art technology is also a drawcard for university students.

Final-year radiation therapy student Thyda Rim has travelled up from Melbourne for all her placements.

"You would think that advanced technology like this you can only find in metro areas, but it's pretty cool that you can access it here in more remote communities," she said.

"I don't know where I'm going next, so having this opportunity to work with great technology was a plus for me."

Ms Rim came to Dubbo after hearing about the advanced technology and friendly staff. (ABC Western Plains: Lily Plass )

Dr Delaney said RAD is the future of radiation therapy for more providers nationwide.

"Radiotherapy is evolving over time, so you would expect even better improvements in the future."

title: Commonwealth Bank boss says Reserve Bank rate hikes probably finished
text:
The chief executive of Australia's largest bank, Matt Comyn, says CBA believes the Reserve Bank has finished hiking interest rates for now, but the board's November meeting is "live" and another rise remains a possibility.

Speaking with the ABC's Alan Kohler, the Commonwealth Bank chief executive said the next movement of the RBA would depend on the quarterly inflation data released at the end of the month.

"We believe that's the last [rate rise], but certainly I think the last meeting of this calendar year is live," he said.

"We see and feel … the impact of higher rates. We feel that customers obviously are feeling the increasing burden from higher rates.

Mr Comyn said the September hike was needed due to rising inflationary pressures from global forces such as the Middle East conflict and fuel price rises.

Loading...

He said cost-of-living pressures were affecting different cohorts of CBA customers in different ways.

"We're seeing … where people are exposed particularly to higher borrowing costs and higher mortgages, a reduction in spending in some instances, [a] reduction in terms of savings," he said.

"I think households are feeling the pressure. We saw an increase in, for example, the proportion of customers that are requiring financial assistance or struggling to meet repayments.

"There are some subsectors, let's say in business, which are starting to feel the pressure of less consumer and household demand and expenditure."

Comyn says housing will bounce back

But there have been pockets of hope, with the bank seeing a 13 per cent growth in business lending across the 2026 financial year.

Doubtful debts were also still low and "well below where you would expect the average to be", mostly because unemployment was still low, he said.

Housing is also an area of optimism, with Mr Comyn predicting Australia's tanking property prices will bounce back.

RBA hikes interest rates to 4.6pc The Reserve Bank increases interest rates to 4.6 per cent in its fourth rate rise this year.

He recalled that when interest rates last peaked in 2023, house prices fell nationally by 8.2 per cent, and compared it to current predictions of an estimated 10 per cent drop.

"I seem to remember considerably less focus on house prices during that time. But yes, I do think house prices will weaken over the course of this year," he said.

Consequently, he said, if interest rates reduced through next year as expected, property prices would pick up again in line with rising demand that was also bolstered by a "structural undersupply of housing".

"Housing is a very important asset in Australia. I think it's 57 per cent of household wealth in the country," he said.

"The biggest issue over the long term is our inability to grow productivity in terms of the production of housing."

Reduce regulation to grow the pie

Mr Comyn added his voice to calls for Australia to boost its productivity, saying a rate of 3 per cent compared to 2 per cent made "a really big difference".

"Productivity is what enables you to earn on an ongoing basis the income to be able to support improvement in in living standards," he said.

He said this was achieved through housing, low-cost energy, skills, migration and technological advancements including AI.

What's impacted in the RBA rate hike While the RBA's decisions are most felt through mortgage repayments, their impact extends well beyond home loans.

"We need to make it easier for small businesses or new businesses to be created that are successful and productive. And I think that's very hard in the current context," he said.

"Where I would be focusing on most is all on the supply-side reform. How do we reduce layers of approvals? How do we reduce layers of, in some areas, regulation? How do we accelerate a number of those processes.

"It's much easier to distribute a growing pie than one that isn't."

The federation is a bad business

Mr Comyn said fragmentation across both the Commonwealth and the states was particularly problematic in the context of regulation.

"It's the same inside a company; you're often adding an extra control, an extra process," he said.

"It's much harder to actually look at the totality and work out whether there's complete coherence, if there's anything there that's waste.

" If the federation was a company, I don't think you'd invest in it. "

Mr Comyn said there were examples where the states were working very constructively with the Commonwealth but said there needed to be "real urgency across a number of these topics".

The banking boss said worried about the federal government running deficits "particularly at this point in time".

Banks respond to RBA Australia's big four banks announce interest rate rises after the Reserve Bank of Australia lifted the cash rate to its highest level in more than a decade.

"Typically over a decade, there's times when the economic conditions are better and you should be able to run a surplus," he said.

"You're then creating fiscal capacity and degrees of freedom for some form of exogenous shock

"We're seeing a big increase in fiscal deficits around the world. I think this is reducing degrees of freedom.

"This puts a lot of pressure on future generations in particular."

More volatility the new norm

Like RBA governor Michele Bullock, Mr Comyn said he had also noticed frequent and potentially larger volatility.

"So for these shocks, we have a number of structural challenges as well, including demographics, how we actually deliver the services that Australians expect today and reasonably demand for the future," he said.

Matt Comyn says Australia needs to boost productivity. (Reuters: Hollie Adams)

Mr Comyn also weighed in on defence spending, saying he supported raising how much the country allocated.

"There's no question we're in a different geopolitical and national security environment," he said.

"We've got to be able to pay for that. Obviously, we need to spend that well. But I find it challenging looking at all of the budget papers and documents and trying to work out how to chart that course. And those trade-offs are not easy to achieve now."

title: How a determined English woman planted the seeds for beloved flower festival
text:
Once a rubbish-filled paddock, Corbett Gardens in Bowral was opened in 1914 after Ada Corbett campaigned for a public garden with a bandstand at its centre.

For generations, it has been a place for locals to gather and enjoy the NSW Southern Highlands seasons.

For more than six decades, it has also been home to the Tulip Time Festival.

According to local historian Linda Emery, Ada Corbett moved to Australia to help her sister run a ladies' college at Burradoo Park.

"She married a naval commander called Watties Corbett, had one daughter and he then died almost straight away, so she was left a widow with a child very early on," Ms Emery said.

The annual tulip festival has manifested many activities, including Tulips After Dark. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

After moving to town, Ms Corbett began campaigning to beautify Bowral.

"The paddock near her home, where the Corbett Gardens were established, was pretty terrible," Ms Emery said.

"Called Denmead's Paddock, it was full of rubbish and an eyesore."

Corbett Gardens, with its bandstand, was first proposed in 1910 by Ada Corbett, circa 1920s. (Supplied: Berrima District Historical Society)

Ms Corbett appealed for government help in 1910, and the council acquired the land the following year.

The gardens were named after her in 1914, although by that time she had already moved to Norfolk Island.

Loading...

Tulip Town

Tulip Time began in 1961 with a Rotary Club donation of 500 bulbs.

It has since become one of Australia's best-known flower festivals.

Although Linda Emery loves Tulip Time, she avoids the gardens during the festival.

"There's too many people there, and I think most locals tend to not go to town during Tulip Time because you can't get a parking spot," she said.

"Other than that, I think it's terrific for the town because it brings people to area and makes them aware of the other things we have to offer."

For a couple of years before Tulip Time, Bowral held a Festival of Flowers including this street parade in 1959. (Supplied: Berrima District Historical Society)

Pretty as a picture

Sourced annually from Tasmania, the bulbs are chosen for their differing features, with 40 varieties included in this year's festival.

"We've got mixes of orange and yellows called strong golds, and the Fabio, which is one of my favourite bulbs," said Fabian Monteleone, head of the horticulture crew at Wingecarribee Shire Council.

Fabian Monteleone has been working on Tulip Time for the past six years. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

Cockatoos, possums and rats have been known to damage the displays, leaving the gardening crew to replace plants and protect those that remain.

Mr Monteleone joked that he became a "movable scarecrow" as he tried to keep wildlife away from the flower beds.

"This is just gardening and we've got to adjust to nature, to the seasons and to the wildlife," he said.

It takes a crew of gardeners to plant and maintain Southern Highlands parks and gardens. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

"I've got photos of my mum walking through here in the 60s and to think of the amount of people that have come here and used this park, it's very special, and I'm quite proud to be working here.

"But it's quite a tired park, there's been a lot of foot traffic, so after this festival, I hope that Corbett Gardens will be having a rest for a couple of years."

Then and now

A recent review of Tulip Time recommended keeping the festival at Corbett Gardens while spreading more activities across the Southern Highlands to ease pressure on the park.

The review found the gardens were deteriorating under the weight of the event, which drew more than 70,000 attendees in both 2024 and 2025.

It also found some locals felt Tulip Time had become more of a tourism product than a community celebration, and that the council needed better evidence of its economic benefits and its effect on residents.

Many photos were taken with the beautiful crab apple tree that once stood as a centrepiece in Corbett Gardens Bowral. (ABC Illawarra: Sarah Moss)

With some trees at least 100 years old, new features are taking shape across the park.

"We're losing centrepieces like the beautiful crab apple that came down in a storm last year, so it's important we're planting for future generations to enjoy as well," Mr Monteleone said.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and teal MP Allegra Spender have made a rare unified demand after the taxation office announced its plan to ban the use of credit cards for the payment of tax bills. Industry Minister Tim Ayres on Friday defended the move, blaming “profiteering” credit card companies for forcing the Australian Taxation Office’s hand amid growing anger on social media over Labor’s banning of card surcharges. Community Strong Australia MP Allegra Spender. Alex Ellinghausen The Reserve Bank of Australia on Thursday banned surcharges for Mastercard, Visa and eftpos networks, after a campaign from Labor the government said would save consumers $1.6 billion a year. As of October 1 merchants can no longer charge additional fees on checkout, which the Albanese government argues will save consumers money at the till. The move immediately prompted backlash from small business operators who say they will be forced to pass along charges to consumers in the upfront cost of goods and services. The RBA argues the transfer of charges to product pricing will inflate costs by around 0.1 per cent.

Advertisement

The tax office subsequently announced a plan to ban credit card transactions from November 30, saying in a statement: “As a government agency, the ATO has decided it would not be appropriate for the cost of credit card merchant fees to be transferred to the community,” an agency statement reads. The tax office said only 2.3 per cent of tax payments were made with credit cards in the 2024-25 financial year, and that 60 per cent of those charges were made by large organisations. “The credit card companies are charging too much, and that is a charge, ultimately, on the taxpayers because the ATO has to pay it. It’s a charge on Australian taxpayers. It’s not the right thing to do,” Ayres told News24 on Friday. “There are alternative ways of paying, and the ATO will work through that with their customers and their stakeholders.”

Advertisement

Spender on Friday called for the decision to be reversed, saying the ATO was acting hypocritically. “I’m hearing that all the time from people in my community who are small business [owners], and it’s particularly cash flow that is really hard to manage. So this is where I think the ATO should reverse this,” Spender told Nine’s Today show on Friday. Related Article Payments Cash discounts and refunds: Your card surcharge ban cheat sheet One Nation leader Pauline Hanson echoed Spender’s comments, saying the move was an “unintended consequence because [Labor] never think anything through”, as she joined calls from the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry for the decision’s reversal. “Businesses are expected to absorb these fees, while the ATO avoids them by withdrawing credit-card payments,” Hanson said.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said the government was “insensitive”, as he sought to blame the decision on a lack of business experience from Labor MPs. “On the day that [Labor] impose these surcharges on small businesses, has decided that the ATO won’t take credit card payments because they don’t want the surcharges. I mean, seriously, you couldn’t make it up,” Taylor said. Several social media posts have gone viral accusing the government of inadvertently inflating the price of products, comically depicting business owners rolling merchant fees into the base cost of products. text:

SportNRLNRLW 2026 Why Broncos have ‘freakish’ rival to thank for their lethal spine Nick Wright October 2, 2026 — 2:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It took an impassioned plea from one of the NRLW’s leading superstars to entice Jada Ferguson back to rugby league, and on the cusp of a second premiership ring. The Brisbane Broncos hooker had been aged out of the game after under-12s, with her Toowoomba home town short of opportunities for girls beyond that. Broncos NRLW hooker Jada Ferguson. NRL Images She instead tried her hand at rugby sevens, before Queensland Maroons superstar Tarryn Aiken – who will line up against Ferguson for the Roosters in Sunday’s grand final – got in her ear. “Exactly,” Ferguson laughed, when put to her that if she helped inspire a Broncos triumph – having scored in last year’s decider – it would partly be by Aiken’s doing.

Advertisement

“I didn’t come back to rugby league until I was 18 when I moved down to the Gold Coast for university. We played touch together, and she said ‘come to league, come to league’,” Ferguson said. “I played with her at Tweed Seagulls, and then in my first year of league I made under-19s Origin and then got selected in the Broncos squad. She’s had a big impact on getting me over to rugby league, so it’s exciting to verse her and hopefully beat them. “She helps me to be confident in myself. She’s just a good mentor as well as a player, she does so well in the game and her eyes-up footy is unreal … she can make and break a game, she pulls off stuff that is pretty freakish.” Jada Ferguson and Tarryn Aiken playing for the Broncos together in 2021. NRL Images The pair have gone on to represent Queensland together, featuring in the 2025 series defeat. Ferguson’s touch football background has seeped into her rugby league career – finishing third for dummy-half runs in 2026 (52) and equal-first across the past three seasons (148) – and has cast her eye towards an Aiken reunion for Australia at this year’s World Cup.

Advertisement

When Ferguson arrived at Red Hill, Aiken was the marquee halfback of the Broncos – inspiring the club’s 2019 and 2020 premierships, the latter against her current Roosters outfit. Her fullback on that day was Tamika Upton, who will now chase her sixth NRLW premiership – a fourth for the Broncos, having won consecutive titles with the Newcastle Knights. Upton has been heralded the best player in the women’s rugby league space, with three Dally M Medals to show for it, but there is a strong case for Aiken to be considered in similar regard. Jada Ferguson, pictured being tackled by Olivia Kernick, has become a State of Origin star and Broncos premiership champion since being drawn back to rugby league. Getty Images “She’s an incredible player, I played a lot with her, and she’s probably the brains, but she’s also got the strike as well. She’s got the talent to get through the line, but she’s also one of the most talented at setting up other people around her, which is why they’re such a good team,” Upton said.

Advertisement

“It [our relationship] actually goes way back, I actually played a bit of touch football with Tarryn as well in our junior years, so I’ve known her for a very long time. It’s no coincidence she’s as good as she is; she works very hard, and she’s a very diligent trainer.” Brisbane edge forward and fellow Maroon Romy Teitzel added: “We’ve seen what Tarryn can do single-handedly for the Roosters, Jillaroos, and even alongside her in the Queensland arena. “She creates opportunities out of nothing, so she’ll be very dangerous for us, but she’s one player out of 17 who take the field for them this weekend. I also like my halfbacks as well, they can create some pretty cool opportunities.” Loading Having missed last year’s decider between the powerhouse clubs due to a knee injury, Aiken – who became the first player to be named in the Players’ Dream Team for a fifth time this year – is now out to ensure the career of retiring former teammate, Ali Brigginshaw, does not end on a high note.

Advertisement

She will enter the decider fresh off scoring the match-winning try against the Canberra Raiders to seal a preliminary final victory in an undefeated campaign, as Sydney seek to extract revenge from Brisbane’s 22-18 victory in 2025. “I’m just really proud to see her out there, I know she’s an enemy on Sunday, but she’s also been a teammate of mine, and to see her go down last year hurt. To see her back out there, we’d rather take on the best,” Brigginshaw said of the 27-year-old. “She’s a big game player and performing very highly. She directs that team, but they’ve got Tarryn Aiken, and we’ve got Jesse Southwell, so it’s the battle of the sevens out there, and that’s what I’m excited to see – two of the best going at it.” Stepping into Aiken’s old jersey this year has been arguably the brightest light in the NRLW, with Southwell relishing the challenge, before watching her childhood club – the Knights – end a 25-year wait between NRL grand final appearances.

“I, personally, didn’t think I’d be alive to see it, which is crazy. Newcastle would be buzzing right now, and it was buzzing when we made those grand finals,” Southwell said. The 21-year-old has gone on to hoist the silverware twice with Newcastle, guided New South Wales to State of Origin glory, represented Australia three times, and even won gold in rugby sevens at the 2022 Commonwealth Games. Jesse Southwell will seek to become a dual-club premiership-winner after guiding Newcastle to consecutive titles in 2021 and 2022. title: ANZ drops KPMG as auditor after almost 60 years
text:
ANZ has dropped KPMG after almost 60 years of the firm holding the $29.3 million contract to audit the bank’s accounts, in a fresh blow to the consulting firm that continues to contend with the fallout from a damaging whistleblower scandal.

An anonymous KPMG whistleblower warned the firm of a raft of serious allegations, including that senior partners had misused confidential information to win work, but was given short shrift until Senator Deborah O’Neill went public with the allegations in March.

ANZ has ditched KPMG as its auditors after they worked together since 1969. Bloomberg

That has led to companies including Macquarie Bank ditching KPMG as their auditors in a series of repercussions that escalated on Friday when ANZ announced its board had also decided to open up its contract for tender.

“ANZ’s external audit service has been provided by KPMG since 1969,” a spokesman said. He attributed the bank’s decision to the length of time KPMG had worked with the bank, and did not mention the whistleblower scandal that has led to numerous senior staff leaving and mass layoffs.

title: New student visa crackdown comes with extra cost for course-switchers
text:
In Brief Students switching education providers will have to pay a new visa fee, expected to cost about half the original visa fee.

Student visa application fees have also risen from $1,600 to $2,000.

New rules for international students are in force, aimed at stopping so-called 'visa-hopping' by limiting course changes and curtailing how family members can join them in Australia.

Students wanting to change education providers will need to apply for a new visa, starting next year, which will cost over $2,000.

Labor's plan to bring net overseas migration down to a budget target of 225,000 by 2028 will be partly fulfilled by closing onshore pathways from temporary visas to student visas, Assistant Citizenship Minister Julian Hill told a migration conference on Friday.

"People will no longer be able to apply for a student visa while in Australia from working holidaymaker visas, training visas, temporary employer visas and so on," he said.

The plan includes banning student and graduate visa holders from bringing their families unless they are on government scholarships, PhD students or from Pacific and ASEAN countries. The new family rules mean that dependants can only be added after their visa is granted.

"Families already in Australia will be grandfathered as an exception as the government is not in the business of breaking up families already here," Hill said.

From July next year, students switching education providers will need to apply for a new visa, expected to cost about half the original visa fee, estimated at around $2,500.

The new visa will retain the original end date and can only be issued if students move into equivalent or higher qualifications.

International students who swap courses will have to complete 12 months instead of the current six while the new visa regime is set up.

"Australia welcomes genuine students seeking a premium Australian education but the government will not back down from seeking to manage the size and the shape of the onshore student market," Hill said.

Student visa rejections hit record levels in August at 35 per cent, up 12 per cent on the same month last year.

Students can extend their visa to complete a course if they fall sick, fail a subject or their course provider goes out of business.

After completing a course, they can apply for a new student visa, but it must be ranked higher in the Australian Qualifications Framework (AQF). Moving from higher education to higher VET courses will not be allowed.

Independent MP Allegra Spender told SBS News that temporary visa holders have grown from 1.8 million to 2.8 million in a decade, which is supported by Department of Home Affairs figures.

"That's not sustainable, economically or socially," Spender said.

"International students bring enormous value. But in some universities their growth has coincided with a declining student experience.

"The government must get the settings right, and universities must build a shared campus life, so it's a genuine exchange. Limits to family visas for international students and restrictions on visa hopping are sensible. The question is why these settings are new," she said.

"Every migration choice is a trade-off, and Australians deserve a say in making them. The crossbench will take those trade-offs directly to our communities ... I suspect we'll find far more common ground than the loudest voices suggest."

As a transition measure, transfers have been prevented within the first 12 months of commencing a principal course between now and 1 July 2027, when the new transfer visa comes into effect.

Hill also said there will be a "sharpening focus of the skilled migration program" via two new ministerial directions that came into effect last week.

"Priority is now being given to healthcare, construction, teaching, resources, agriculture, aquaculture and fishing, helping direct skills to the parts of the economy where they are needed most," he said.

The Opposition is expected to announce its immigration policy next week, while One Nation plans to limit net overseas migration to 130,000 per year after three years of "negative migration".

title: Which super funds earned a retirement tick of approval?
text:
in brief An industry assessment handed eight ticks of approval to 45 assessed super funds.

Those eight were found to offer their members the best support through their retirement.

Only eight of 45 assessed superannuation funds have received an industry tick of approval for the level of support they provide members throughout retirement.

The 2026 Epic Retirement Tick has been awarded to retirement funds that met at least 14 of an expanded 20 support criteria, up from 18 last year.

The analysis is backed by Chant West, one of Australia's most prominent commercial superannuation research and ratings agencies.

The tick measures how well a fund's investments perform, how competitive its fees are, how innovative its product offerings are, and how comprehensive its member services and advice are.

"Australians have spent decades building their super," said Epic Retirement Institute founder Bec Wilson.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"As they reach retirement, they deserve to understand what their fund can actually do to support them through the years ahead."

The push for better fund support comes as many Australians approach retirement facing significant savings shortfalls.

According to the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia, a single homeowner requires $630,000 and a couple $730,000 in super for a "comfortable" retirement.

However, Australian Taxation Office data reveal that the median super balance for those aged 60 to 64 is just over $200,000 — meaning retirees rely heavily on fund advice, tax strategies, and government pension integration to stretch their savings.

Wilson noted that the tick is not a product ranking or a directive to switch membership.

"The Tick is not a rating, ranking or recommendation of a super fund or financial product. There's no first place, second place or 'best fund'," she said.

Instead, it serves as a tool to help Australians "become a more informed super fund member and customer".

Which super funds received the Epic Retirement Tick?

Of 45 assessed regulated, defined-contribution funds, only eight met the benchmark for the 2026/2027 financial year.

Those were:

AMP Super

ART-Super Savings

Aware Super

Brighter Super

Colonial First State - FirstChoice

Hostplus

UniSuper

Vision Super

These funds performed well in several distinct categories, like tailored pension investment options, digital security, and advice access.

AMP, ART, Aware, Hostplus, and Vision Super were highlighted for allowing pension members to request ad-hoc payments and receive funds on the same day or via immediate OSKO transfers.

Funds like ART, AMP, and UniSuper also stood out for offering dedicated lifetime income options like annuities to provide members with guaranteed retirement income.

READ MORE There's another reason to check who inherits your superannuation

However, industry analysts note that the overall pass rate remains remarkably low.

Writing in Investment Magazine, Chant West general manager Ian Fryer highlighted that, to earn the badge, funds could no longer rely solely on offering specialised retirement products but also had to demonstrate meaningful member engagement.

For example, funds offering lifetime income options were assessed on whether their members were actually taking up those products.

What has changed this year?

Now in its second year, the Epic Retirement Tick has been awarded to three new funds in addition to last year's six — TelstraSuper having merged with Aware. AMP, Colonial, and Vision are all new additions to the benchmark.

The assessment framework has also been updated to target industry difficulties and raise consumer standards. The pass threshold was raised from 12 out of 18 to 14 out of 20, with a new requirement that funds have no outstanding regulatory enforcement actions.

The expanded 2026 criteria introduced tougher hurdles around digital service delivery, complaints management, and cybersecurity protections.

Investment performance criteria were refined to focus on a seven-year evaluation window, rather than 10 years, to allow a stronger emphasis on non-investment support features.

"Some have really stepped up to the plate," Wilson said. "Others are still working towards the standard, and there remains a meaningful gap between what some funds currently provide and what the criteria ask of them."

The Epic Retirement Tick is a proprietary badge issued by a private research firm, not a binding compliance benchmark.

It is separate to statutory government assessment through the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority.
