title: The card surcharge ban is in force. Now Australians are questioning new fees
text:
In brief Consumers have raised concerns about whether new fees will effectively take the place of card surcharges.

Following an RBA review, businesses can no longer charge customers a surcharge for paying by card.

It took just hours for fresh frustrations to emerge after Australia's card surcharge ban came into effect on Thursday.

Consumers on social media questioned new charges appearing at checkouts online, including some described as "platform" or service fees.

Some said they had encountered the charges in transactions made after new rules came into force preventing businesses from imposing surcharges on credit and debit card payments, prompting questions about whether other fees were effectively taking their place.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) told SBS News it was "aware of concerns about businesses introducing fees described as platform, booking or service fees" since the card surcharge ban took effect.

But the regulator said such fees are not necessarily prohibited.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Whether a charge is a genuine fee for a particular service or amounts to a "card payment surcharge by another name" depends on what it covers and how it operates, an ACCC spokesperson said.

The new rules do not prevent businesses from charging genuine fees for services such as ordering or booking platforms.

However, under Australian Consumer Law, businesses cannot mislead customers about their prices, including the nature or reason for an additional fee or whether it is optional.

Businesses must also display the total minimum price of a product as a single figure, including mandatory fees that can be calculated in advance.

The card surcharge ban followed a Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) review into card payment costs and surcharging that found removing them would support a more efficient and competitive payments system.

"When card surcharging ends, the sticker price will be the price that consumers end up paying," the RBA website explained.

In other words, if an item is advertised at $100, consumers should expect to pay $100 at the checkout with either cash or a card.

'Teething issues'

Australian Payments Network chief strategy officer Rajat Jain said a "change of this scale is not immune to some teething issues".

Card networks like Visa and Mastercard, as well as payment service providers, are responsible for administering and enforcing the no-surcharge rules.

Businesses will still have costs associated with processing card payments, but they're no longer permitted to add them as an extra fee.

Businesses may choose to reflect those costs in their overall pricing.

"Shoppers shouldn't assume today’s surcharge ban means they'll now start paying less," said Sally Tindall, data insights director of financial comparison site Canstar.

"Businesses still have to pay to accept card payments, so some may choose to build those costs into their prices instead."

For some business owners, the changes have prompted difficult decisions.

David Bitton, owner of the Bitton Rose Bay cafe in Sydney, said more than 90 per cent of his sales are made via card.

With surcharges no longer an option, he estimated the change could cost his business as much as $40,000.

"So I've got to be clever and strategise how I'm gonna pass on that cost, without upsetting people basically," he told SBS News.

Rather than raising menu prices, Bitton said he's increasing his weekend surcharge fee from 10 to 12 per cent.

The RBA says the changes only apply to surcharges specifically added for customers paying by card; booking fees, service fees and hospitality surcharges for weekends and public holidays are permitted.

Concerned about a fee you've been charged?

Consumers who believe they are still being charged a fee specifically because they paid by card should first seek clarification from the business and ask for the surcharge to be refunded, the ACCC said.

Concerns about ongoing card surcharges can also be raised with the relevant card network or payment service provider.

Jain from the Australian Payments Network said businesses that continue to impose prohibited card surcharges may be directed by their bank or payment provider to remove them and could face penalties.

Meanwhile, concerns about misleading fees or pricing — including a failure to display the total minimum price as a single figure — can be reported to the ACCC or the relevant state or territory consumer protection agency.

The surcharge ban covers EFTPOS, Visa and Mastercard, including credit, debit and prepaid cards.

American Express and UnionPay are also removing surcharges from 1 October, while PayPal's equivalent change takes effect on 5 October.

The rules generally apply whether the card was issued in Australia or overseas, although individual network rules and exemptions can apply.

The change applies to both online and in-store transactions.

title: The cockpit question at the heart of the flydubai incident
text:
in brief Passengers were able to access the cockpit of the Flydubai flight as it tumbled from the sky.

Aviation industry experts say the incident raises further questions around airline safety.

This article contains references to suicide.

As authorities attempt to make sense of the flydubai flight that briefly dropped from the sky on Wednesday, a key question will be how passengers were able to enter the cockpit and deal with the threat within it.

The incident, which occurred on a passenger plane travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv in Israel, has raised questions over industry safety.

Since the September 11 attacks, global airline policies have been completely transformed and keeping passengers out of the cockpit was a key focus.

Now, attention will no doubt be turned to the procedures in place to mitigate risks arising from within the flight deck itself — screening and procedures around pilot health and safety will come under scrutiny.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Some of the 174 passengers and crew on board the flydubai flight were able to regain control after the pilot, Indian national Smit Machchhar, was allegedly stabbed by his co-pilot, who sent the plane into a sharp descent.

As it dropped more than 5km in a matter of minutes, passengers breached the cockpit, took control of the plane, and restrained the co-pilot who had the controls.

The Israeli government has described the incident as a "hijacking" after the emergency call was made from the cockpit by the injured pilot, but flydubai has cautioned against jumping to conclusions. The airline temporarily suspended travel to and from Israel pending a multinational investigation into the incident.

How did passengers manage to breach the cockpit?

Aviation security expert Tony Stanton said access to a passenger plane cockpit should not be possible.

"Whilst the door is not impenetrable, it is highly unlikely that you're able to get through that door," Stanton said.

"Since September 11, there were significant changes to cockpit door security ... it was actually a standard introduced by the United States."

Passengers on board the aircraft said the door to the cockpit — a term which originates in 16th century cock fighting and has been adapted from naval terminology — was open when they approached it.

The Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after a violent altercation in the cockpit. Source: Getty / Erik Marmor

"The door apparently wasn't locked and we managed to open it somehow," passenger Yaniv Hayoun told reporters.

Hayoun later told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that as others tied up the attacker, "I jumped back, grabbed the controls, and started pulling back the handles", before other crew members took over.

Stanton said pilots in the cockpit typically need to press a button inside to open the door. He suspects Machchhar was able to do this while injured.

Former A380 Airbus captain James Nixon said the pilot had "amazing" presence of mind in thinking to open the door after having been stabbed.

"Even if the cabin crew wanted to get in to help, they would firstly go through a procedure where the pilots have to let them in," he told ABC News on Thursday.

"There's another procedure that takes about 35 or 40 seconds to get in if there's no response.

"So, it would have taken a long time, and by that stage it would have all been over."

Incident shines a light on pilot mental health

While the motivation of the co-pilot in the flydubai incident is unclear, Stanton notes that mental health incidents with pilots are becoming more common.

In 2022 a China Eastern flight carrying 132 people was intentionally plunged into the ground in China by someone in the cockpit, black box data later found, killing everyone on board.

In 2015, a Germanwings flight from Barcelona to Düsseldorf was intentionally directed into the French Alps by its 27-year-old pilot, who had previously been treated for severe suicidal tendencies. All 150 people on board were killed.

READ MORE The 15 minutes that plunged a flydubai flight into chaos: What we know

"They're still very, very rare, but they're starting to happen more often," Stanton said.

Screening for pilot mental health in Australia is governed by the Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA), which relies on a combination of mandatory periodic health assessments and regular examinations conducted by specialist medical teams.

While the process is rigorous and the industry has extensive safety procedures in place to screen for troubled staff, Stanton argued that "a questionnaire on a screen every year" is not sufficient.

"Pilots are afraid of reporting things because if CASA takes away their medical, you don't have a job," he said. "Pilots are incredibly reluctant, sadly, to disclose some things when they go and do this yearly check."

However, he said there is no way to make flying completely risk-free and that aircraft incidents will continue as passenger numbers across the globe are only projected to increase.

"Even if we kept the accident rate the same today, if it's the same in 20 years, we will have more catastrophes simply because we're increasing the amount we fly."

The reforms are part of a tightening of immigration controls by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.

Japan has toughened requirements for foreigners seeking permanent residency as part of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's push to tighten immigration controls.

Previous guidelines did not lay out specific thresholds for income, pension or language skills.

Even though Japan has a rapidly ageing population and is suffering labour shortages in many sectors, opposition to immigration is growing, prompting a push by Takaichi for tighter regulations on foreign nationals.

"As the number of foreign residents in Japan increases, the government is facing the fact that some citizens feel anxiety and a sense of unfairness," Takaichi said in an extended post on X on Sunday, adding that she was pushing for "orderly coexistence" with foreign nationals.

Programs to attract international workers have fuelled public worry.

Anti-immigration sentiment has spread across social media and false claims have circulated widely, including that a significant portion of welfare payments in Japan go to foreigners and that they are making Japanese streets less safe.

Experts and many business leaders warn, however, that Japan must welcome more foreign workers to sustain itself.

Japan needs to open its doors to more foreigners, the Nikkei business daily said in a recent editorial.

"Japan should stop viewing foreigners merely as a temporary labour force and instead promote their long-term settlement by expanding Japanese-language education and improving their treatment," it said.

Anti-immigration sentiment

Foreigners were a major issue in last year's upper house election, which saw the sharp rise of the "Japanese-first" Sanseito party, which describes immigration as a "silent invasion".

The new rules for permanent residency come after the ruling Liberal Democratic Party last year pushed to tighten regulations for business manager visas, meaning entrepreneurs will be forced to leave Japan if they don't meet the new conditions.

Some foreign residents seek permanent residency to secure long-term stability, employment freedom and to earn trust within Japanese society. Those without permanent residency often have difficulty obtaining mortgages, for example.

Thursday's changes may prevent some people from applying for permanent residency but should not immediately push anyone out of the country.

Candidates must also show "understanding" of social rules and demonstrate expected pension benefits equivalent to someone who has paid pension insurance for 30 years.

Having lived in Japan for a decade, permanent residency applicant Chono said he saw both sides of the debate but that the country needed young people "to support its future".

"In recent years, I believe there had been a strong push to promote cultural diversity. The momentum has stalled, perhaps, and maybe it may never fully return."

title: A buyer's market without buyers: Housing downturn deepens with nationwide falls
text:
in brief House prices have fallen 1.1 per cent in September, marking their sixth monthly decline.

The latest data from Cotality suggests widespread national downturn, rather than isolated declining regional markets.

Australian property values fell 1.1 per cent in September, dropping for the sixth consecutive month as the national housing downturn continues to pick up speed.

Cotality's latest home value index report shows overall property values are now 5.2 per cent lower than their March peak, with clearance rates faltering. Houses are sitting on the market for an average of 39 days across capital cities, up from 23 days a year ago.

The property market analysis firm's executive research director, Tim Lawless, said the downturn reflects a "combination of affordability constraints," including higher interest rates, elevated living costs, and weaker consumer sentiment. All of these have "reduced purchasing capacity and dampened buyer demand", Lawless said.

On Tuesday, the Reserve Bank of Australia raised interest rates to their highest level in 15 years, bringing the cash rate to 4.6 per cent, in a bid to tackle persistent inflation. Australian Bureau of Statistics data shows that borrowers are now spending an average of roughly $4,500 per month to service a standard 30-year loan.

"Borrowers are not only facing higher mortgage costs, but also an extended period of elevated living expenses and negative real income growth," Lawless said.

"Together, these pressures are narrowing the pool of buyers able to qualify for a mortgage and reducing the amount they can afford to pay."

Total advertised housing stock increased 23.1 per cent year-on-year, despite fresh listings entering the market, which dropped 9.2 per cent, as sales velocity declined.

"The lift in available stock is improving choice for buyers, but ironically, many prospective buyers don't have the confidence or financial capacity to buy at the moment," Lawless said.

A national downturn

While the market first showed signs of a downturn in the capital cities of Melbourne and Sydney, the scope and scale of the shift has widened to include virtually every market in the country.

In capital city suburbs, 97 per cent recorded a drop in dwelling values over the three months to the end of September. Every capital city recorded a monthly value fall in September, except Darwin, which rose 0.4 per cent.

In Sydney, housing values fell 1.4 per cent last month, and have dropped 8.6 per cent from their peak in February. The current pace of the decline is slightly faster than what was seen during the equivalent phase of the 2022-23 downturn.

"Sydney continues to lead the housing correction ... highlighting how rapid demand has weakened across the nation's largest housing market," Lawless said.

Melbourne property values dropped 0.7 per cent in September and are down 7.2 per cent below their November 2025 peak.

In regional areas, 71 per cent of local sub-markets dropped over the last month, falling 0.7 per cent. However, regional values remain 5.6 per cent higher annually.

Conditions shift in Brisbane

Brisbane saw the sharpest fall of all capital cities in September, dropping 1.5 per cent, outpacing Sydney's decline.

"The result highlights how sharply conditions have shifted in what had previously been one of the strongest performing housing markets," Lawless said.

Brisbane has overtaken Sydney as the capital city with the fastest declining property prices last month. Source: AAP / Jono Searle

Sales volumes have fallen the fastest in major cities which were previously growth leaders in the market. Brisbane is down 27.2 per cent, with Sydney just behind on 26.5 per cent and Perth at 24.2 per cent.

In mid-sized cities, the decline was less pronounced. Perth's home values have dropped 1.2 per cent over the past month while Adelaide fell 1.3 per cent.

Decline still has further to go

While the market is largely being driven by economic conditions, the Cotality report identifies changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax arrangements as having added "another layer of downside risk".

However, high construction costs, driven by inflationary pressures and labour force tightness, continue to suppress new housing supply, stabilising the market. Low unemployment rates are also preventing widespread selling, the report finds.

Speaking to ABC News on Thursday morning, Lawless said the property market is a buyer's market without buyers.

"Seller numbers are right down and I think that this really reflects the confidence in the housing market and the broader economy and cost of living pressures and high interest rates," he said. "So for now, even though it is a buyer's market, the missing piece of the puzzle is actually buyers."

Lawless pointed to the federal budget as having sent "a shudder" through the housing market, something Labor has frequently denied, and said that even bargain-hunters are staying away out of expectation that the market will continue to decline until interest rates drop.

The country's four largest trading banks all predict that interest rates will remain at their current level, if not higher, with the cycle starting to come down well into next year.

"It's pretty clear that headwinds facing demand are outweighing those supply-side challenges," Lawless said.

"That will be the case, I think, for at least going into 2027 — probably around the middle of next year."

title: Thriving Kids launches today. Here's what parents should know
text:
In brief The government has argued there are more people on the NDIS than originally intended.

The $4 billion program will be co-funded by state, territory and federal governments.

On 1 October, the first stage of Thriving Kids begins to roll out. This new program, announced just over a year ago, is part of the federal government’s sweeping changes to the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS).

It means children aged eight and under, who have developmental delay or autism and low to moderate support needs, will increasingly receive support outside the NDIS, through Thriving Kids. The $4 billion program will be co-funded by state, territory and federal governments.

But this doesn’t mean children are being moved off the NDIS today. Changes to NDIS access won't begin until January 2028.

So, what will Thriving Kids provide? And — after more than a year of negotiation, consultation and controversy — what questions remain?

How did we get here?

The government has argued there are more people on the NDIS than originally intended, and the scheme’s budget is growing too quickly.

One group the government says is particularly over-represented is children under 15. They make up just under half of all NDIS participants. One in two new entrants to the scheme is under nine — many with autism or developmental delay — and across the country one in ten six-year-olds receives NDIS support.

There is also mounting concern the scheme doesn’t serve all these young children well.

The government has argued these children would benefit more from strong, mainstream and community services, rather than an individual NDIS package.

But there wasn’t much initial detail

When Thriving Kids was announced in August 2025 there was relatively little detail. This caused considerable anxiety among families and disability advocates.

Since then — after an advisory process, a parliamentary inquiry, and lengthy negotiations between the Commonwealth and states and territories — we know more about the program.

The proposed national model will combine broad, or universal, supports with more targeted assistance for children who need additional help. Support will respond to children's needs rather than simply depend on a diagnosis, recognising that children's developmental and support needs are not static but can change over time.

So, how will Thriving Kids work?

Currently, children on the NDIS are assessed individually and receive a certain amount of funding their family can use to access services such as speech therapy or visits to a psychologist.

But Thriving Kids will provide supports where children are already going about their lives: in schools and early childhood centres, as well as community spaces (such as libraries or organised sport) and health care. These are known as foundational supports.

Some foundational supports will be universal, meaning they are available to all children and families. These include providing information about child development and linking families to services.

Some universal supports will begin on 1 October — such as supported playgroups for children aged five and under — or shortly after, such as the Medicare-funded health check for three-year-olds, done by GPs and rolling out in November.

Some supports will be targeted to kids' specific needs and provided by allied health professionals, such as occupational therapists, speech pathologists and physiotherapists. These will require some form of assessment to access.

Children with permanent and significant disability, including children with high support needs, will continue to be eligible for the NDIS.

State and territory governments will take the lead on designing and commissioning services that are appropriate to their local population. But Queensland is yet to sign up, so important questions remain about how this will work.

What have some of the sticking points been?

Important questions about Thriving Kids' implementation remain.

One of the biggest challenges has been working out who is responsible for providing and paying for supports outside the NDIS. This problem predates Thriving Kids.

In 2023, the NDIS Review argued the NDIS had blown out its estimates so much because states and territories had moved away from providing disability supports, forcing people to seek NDIS support.

Foundational supports — jointly funded by all governments — are meant to be part of the solution. Thriving Kids is the first program of this kind to be launched.

But while states and territories initially signed up to the federal government’s new model, the relationship has become more fractious as plans have developed.

And while the other states and territories have signed on to deliver Thriving Kids and are developing plans about what these will look like in their communities, Queensland is yet to sign up.

At the moment we don’t know what this will mean for younger children with low-to-moderate needs in Queensland. For example, some aspects of Thriving Kids’ first stage will be rolled out, focusing on general supports. But it’s unclear whether targeted services will be developed.

What do we still need to know?

The Queensland minister for disability services, Amanda Camm, has previously said the federal government has not sufficiently defined what it means by developmental delay or different levels of support needs. She argues the federal government simply wants to shift costs to the states and territories.

The Queensland government shares a concern with a number of disability advocates: that children and families might fall between gaps in services if they’re no longer eligible for the NDIS but can’t get the specific support they need through Thriving Kids.

NDIS eligibility is set to tighten, with the government seeking to cut 160,000 participants from the scheme over the next four years.

So what will happen for families whose children age out of Thriving Kids — at nine — but aren’t eligible for NDIS support? This is a key concern.

The kind of early intervention offered by Thriving Kids is important, but for most children their support needs won’t disappear as they age.

The government has floated the idea of a Thriving Teens scheme, but there are no solid plans yet.

What happens next?

This first stage of Thriving Kids focuses on general universal supports, such as information and advice for families who have concerns about their child’s development, and supported playgroups for children aged five and under.

From January 2027, states and territories will start to develop and roll out targeted supports. These are for children who need additional support, for example, low-cost assistive technologies or speech therapy.

The NDIS will not change its eligibility criteria until January 2028, meaning children will continue to be admitted to the scheme until these changes take place.

Catherine Smith is a senior lecturer of wellbeing science at the Melbourne Graduate School of Education at the University of Melbourne. She receives funding from the NDRP and Australian governments.

title: 'We don't understand': Little-noticed change could hit millions of Australian websites
text:
in brief New rules that could make it more difficult to register .com.au websites have been proposed.

However, other experts suggest the changes will not be as dramatic as they are being made out to be.

A quiet policy shift within Australia's web address regulatory body has industry experts concerned that millions of local websites could be pushed offline, even as the government urges a wait-and-see approach.

Last month, the board of the .au Domain Administrator (auDA) approved "in-principle" recommendations from an independent panel that would overhaul eligibility rules for domestic website registrations.

The decision, recently announced by auDA, will see the long-standing "close and substantial connection" rule scrapped. Companies and organisations will soon no longer be able to register web addresses based on products, services, or events, but will instead have to link their websites to their name alone.

Domain industry experts estimate that "potentially millions" of Australian websites could be impacted and that "confidence" in the .com.au domain address could be shaken if the proposed changes go ahead.

auDA said in a statement to SBS News that rule changes have yet to be finalised and that "most" domain name holders are expected to meet the new requirements.

Under the current rules, businesses are allowed to register website names that are related to their services — such as applepies.com.au for a bakery — but under the new rules, they could need a much more closely aligned Australian company name to match the site.

"The independent review recommendation is intended to strengthen the connection between a com.au or net.au domain name and the domain name holder's official business identity, helping maintain the trust Australians place in .au domain names," the auDa statement said.

"The Panel found the current criteria can create inconsistency in how the allocation rules are applied, can be seen as unfair to small businesses, and in some instances may result in consumer harm."

'More red tape'

Former auDa chair and domain lawyer Erhan Karabardak voted against the change on the divided advisory panel. He said the policy "throws the baby out with the bathwater" and will fail to address the problem it was designed to.

"We still don't understand what the justification was," Karabardak said.

He said the policy change stems from a desire to curb domain investors and "monetised" web portfolios from claiming generic domain names to sell them to legitimate businesses.

However, he argued commercial domain investors will simply work around the change by registering multi-word business names with the Australian Securities and Investments Commission and that everyday users will end up paying more.

"Whenever a business wants to register a generic name, product, or service, they're going to have to firstly pay for a business name — $47 a year — and then pay for a domain name," he said. "It's effectively doubling the cost of registering a .com.au or .net.au domain name."

Schools, charities, and small businesses that want a temporary domain name to promote an event could struggle to do so under the new rules.

Registrants will see the process as "more red tape" and opt to use a different domain address like .com where there are fewer rules, Karabardak said.

Improving trust in the age of AI

While the announcement of the change has sparked concern among industry insiders, some have urged caution until the full details are known.

Patrick Myles, an independent domain industry consultant, told SBS News that he expects the number of registrants who might be impacted will be "pretty small" and that updates to business organisational practices are a routine part of day-to-day operations.

"I'm in this category myself," Myles said. "I have multiple domains, and some of them are less associated with my business than others so [the changes] might impact me a bit, but it doesn't worry me at all."

READ MORE OpenAI apologises for AI models that breached Australian government websites

In an era of declining trust in global institutions and declining relevance of domain names as artificial intelligence changes how users access the internet, Myles said protection of national domain names is increasingly important.

"If you don't support the policies around your country code ... it basically becomes existential," Myles said.

Myles, who has worked for auDA previously, said the changes proposed are "one of the best ways to ensure that the brand of .au is retained and it is kept as strong as it can be in a very, very cloudy world".

While the requirements for registering a .com.au domain could become stricter, Myles advises anyone who fails to meet the new standards to register an .au address, which has fewer requirements.

title: Rates were this high 15 years ago. Here's why it hurts more now
text:
IN BRIEF The size of the average home loan has greatly increased since 2011.

Economists say that while interest rate hikes hurt, high inflation would have worse implications.

When the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) lifted the cash rate by 0.25 percentage points to 4.6 per cent, it brought interest rates to their highest in 15 years.

The economic climate in 2011 was vastly different to today and interest rates are about where the comparison ends.

The average home loan has more than doubled since then, and the average house price has increased from 115 to 130 per cent, varying by state and territory.

Richard Holden, professor of economics at the University of New South Wales, said rising property prices meant households were carrying more debt on average.

"Any given increase in interest rates has much more of an effect than it did 15 years ago," he told SBS News.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"The Reserve Bank seems to have really pivoted to tackling inflation more seriously, and that's going to take most likely another couple of rate rises ... it's just the beginning of more pain for those households."

Wages haven't moved at the same pace as rising house prices and the cost of entering the market has exploded.

The average mortgage in 2011 was equivalent to around 5.4 years of average full-time earnings, while it's now closer to 6.7 years.

In 2011, the average loan size for a first-home buyer was $281,100, according to data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).

Changes to the ABS data collection for Housing Finance data were made in 2019, producing a "level shift" in the available historical data. The ABS said the figures "remained conceptually similar to those published in the existing publication, but with improved quality". Source: SBS News

In 2026, that figure is $731,000, ranging from $516,000 on average in Tasmania to $842,000 in NSW, according to ABS and Canstar data.

House prices have surged due to a number of factors — RBA researchers have found that increases are driven by demand that consistently outstrips supply.

In a 2024 report, RBA assistant governor Sarah Hunter pointed to population growth as a factor contributing to this demand, calling for a "balancing" of the scales.

But there has been growing interest in how negative gearing and capital gains tax discounts in housing influenced the steep incline in housing prices this century, a hypothesis supported in a 2024 study from the University of New South Wales.

The current average variable rate is between 6.24 and 6.62 per cent for owner-occupiers, meaning the average Australian is spending $4,500 to $4,680 per month on their mortgage.

Assuming banks pass on the change in full, Canstar predicts the average owner-occupier variable rate will climb to 6.49 per cent.

In that case, it isn't just homeowners with mortgages who are impacted — Holden said that while it was difficult to determine due to many competing factors, there was anecdotal evidence suggesting interest rate hikes can be passed down from borrowers to renters.

A 'very different' economy

Warwick McKibbin, emeritus professor of economics and public policy at the Australian National University, says that unlike in 2011, this month's hike comes at a time of high uncertainty for the global economy.

"It's very different," he told SBS News, pointing to what he described as "large waste" in government revenue accumulated amid Australia's early 2000s resources boom, when mining investment surged from historical averages of 1.5 per cent to 9 per cent of GDP by 2012.

"Instead of being saved, like the Norwegians did with their sovereign wealth fund, with all the revenue from the oil boom going into a sovereign wealth fund, we just spent it on government outlays and subsidies."

Because of this, McKibbin said, Australia was now in a "much worse" economic position, in which the pressure of high interest rates would fall on both borrowers and the government.

"We had that opportunity to reduce debt to much lower levels, and we didn't. Now, the government has to service its debt, which is now much larger than it was in 2011."

The RBA has delivered four consecutive interest rate hikes this year, in a bid to bring inflation down.

On Wednesday, Australia's annual headline inflation rate jumped to 4 per cent for the 12 months to August 2026, up 0.5 per cent since July.

McKibbin says regardless of any pain caused by high interest rates, the consequences of high inflation were "far worse".

"Mortgage holders will have to pay more, and mortgages are much bigger than they were back in 2011. So the impact on their individual household budget is going to be more severe."

READ MORE The numbers every mortgage borrower and hopeful buyer should know

But, he said, it was dangerous to look in isolation at who was going to lose, especially in the face of high inflation and its impact on cost of living pressures for people at the lower end of the income scale.

While interest rates would impact many households, McKibbin said Australians would overwhelmingly benefit from inflation coming down and cost increases slowing.

"The reality is that interest rates have to go up when there's too much demand in the economy, and these federal and state governments are responsible," he said.

"It's important that this is done. And the reasons for doing it must be understood by the Australian public."

Holden agreed, saying: "Higher interest payments are going to be tough.

"But if we don't get inflation under control, that really hurts everybody, particularly those at the lower end of the income distribution."

title: Australia's card surcharge ban starts today. Here's everything you need to know
text:
in brief The surcharge ban covers eftpos, Visa and Mastercard, including credit, debit and prepaid cards.

The changes do not affect legitimate booking fees, service fees, delivery charges or hospitality surcharges for weekends and public holidays.

From today, the familiar sting of a card surcharge will disappear for Australians paying with most major cards.

But the changes come with a few catches — and not every checkout fee is going away.

Here’s what consumers need to know.

What exactly changes from today?

From 1 October, businesses can no longer add a separate surcharge simply because a customer pays by card on the affected payment networks.

The change comes through new no-surcharge rules introduced by the card networks and follows a Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) review into card payment costs and surcharging that found removing them would support a more efficient and competitive payments system.

"When card surcharging ends, the sticker price will be the price that consumers end up paying," the RBA website explained.

In other words, if an item is advertised at $100, that's the price you'll pay and you should no longer see an extra card-payment fee added when you tap or insert your card.

Which cards and payment methods are covered?

The surcharge ban covers EFTPOS, Visa and Mastercard, including credit, debit and prepaid cards.

American Express and UnionPay are also removing surcharges from 1 October, while PayPal's equivalent change takes effect on 5 October.

The rules generally apply whether the card was issued in Australia or overseas, although individual network rules and exemptions can apply.

Does the ban apply online as well as in-store?

Yes. The change is about the payment method, not whether you are standing at a shop counter or buying from a website.

So an online retailer cannot simply retain a separate Visa, Mastercard or EFTPOS card surcharge because the transaction happens online. The same principle applies to card payments made through apps and other digital checkout systems.

Can businesses still charge booking fees, service fees or weekend surcharges?

Yes, as the RBA site explained: "The changes only apply to surcharges added because a customer pays by card."

The changes do not affect legitimate booking fees, service fees, delivery charges or hospitality surcharges for weekends and public holidays.

Will this make paying cheaper?

The end of surcharges does not necessarily mean lower prices.

Businesses will still have costs associated with processing card payments, but what's changing is they can no longer add them as an extra fee. They may choose to incorporate them into the total price.

The RBA says, "those costs can be reflected in a business’s overall pricing, rather than charged as a separate surcharge".

Could businesses raise prices instead?

Yes. Businesses are generally free to set and change their prices, as long as they do not mislead customers.

READ MORE How to slash your bills and get money back into your pocket quickly

That means a cafe, retailer, or professional service could increase its standard price to cover payment-processing costs.

Can businesses set minimum spends or stop accepting cards?

Businesses can choose which payment methods they accept and can set minimum card-payment amounts, subject to applicable rules.

So don't assume every business will have to accept your card simply because surcharges are disappearing.

Can businesses offer discounts for paying by cash or another method?

Yes. Businesses can encourage customers to use another payment method by offering a discount rather than imposing a card surcharge.

For example, a business could offer a discount for paying by cash or PayID.

What should you do if you’re still charged a card surcharge?

The consumer watchdog has advice for customers who suspect they've been hit with a card surcharge.

First, check what the fee actually is. It may be a legitimate booking, service or weekend surcharge rather than a card-payment surcharge.

If it appears to be a card surcharge, raise it with the business and ask them to remove the fee or refund it.

"Businesses shouldn’t try to avoid the 'no surcharge' rules … by describing a card payment surcharge as another type of fee or charge," the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) said on its website.

From 1 October, consumers can also raise concerns with the relevant card network or the business's payment provider and can report potentially misleading pricing to the ACCC or their state or territory consumer protection agency.

title: The grand 'chonkion' of this year's Fat Bear Week has been declared

Backpack has emerged victorious as this year's Fat Bear Week champion, the heftiest bear in Alaska's Katmai National Park and Preserve.

The nonprofit running the longstanding contest announced that the bear, known for his pacifist nature, was declared the winner on Wednesday AEST with more than 100,000 votes, narrowly beating Bear 910 with just over 50 per cent of the poll.

Fat Bear Week was established in 2014 as an interactive way to inform the public about brown bears, the coastal cousins of grizzlies.

title: How one pensioner's eviction became a flashpoint in Spain's housing crisis
text:
In brief Spain’s government proposed banning evictions until 2030 and curbing property speculation amid a housing crisis.

An 87-year-old woman whose eviction sparked protests accepted a deal to return to her home.

Spain's coalition government said it had agreed to proposals including banning evictions until 2030 to address the country's housing crisis, as the 87-year-old woman whose forced removal last week triggered protests accepted an offer to return home.

Hundreds of people remained camped in one of Madrid's main squares on Tuesday to protest Maricarmen Abascal's removal from her home on a stretcher last week. They are demanding legal reforms including a rent freeze and the automatic renewal of leases without abusive rent hikes.

Spanish health minister Monica Garcia said the ruling Socialists reached an agreement with junior partner Sumar on Tuesday for a set of new measures, including rolling over contracts until 2028 and banning so-called vulture funds from the housing market.

However, the minority government faces an uphill battle to secure support in a fragmented parliament.

The government was seeking to broaden the definition of what constitutes a vulture fund beyond large private equity funds to any fund or company that buys housing for speculation, housing minister Isabel Rodriguez told a news conference, naming Urbagestion, the small company that evicted Abascal, as an example of a firm that might fall into that category.

The measures will be divided into two decrees to be voted on in parliament later this week, with the majority in a first decree. The "final sticking point" of automatic contract rollover is in a second decree, social affairs minister Pablo Bustinduy told a news conference.

'Time to intervene'

"It is time to intervene in the speculative housing market and start striking a balance between ordinary citizens and vulture funds," Garcia said in a post on X.

Junts, the Catalan pro-independence party that would need to back the decree for it to pass, said on Tuesday it was still far from agreeing on all measures and wanted protection for small landlords, who make up the vast majority of property owners in Spain.

"Lumping together in this category those who have invested their savings in a flat, a restaurant or a property — putting them all in the same basket — is a mistake," she added.

Madrid's tenants' union criticised the government's decision to split the measures into two decrees and said the Madrid encampment and others across Spain would continue until their full demands were met, with further demonstrations planned.

The lawyer for pensioner Abascal said on Tuesday that Urbagestion, the fund that owns her apartment, had offered a preliminary agreement that will allow her return to her home, paying 30 per cent of her pension over the next eight years, equivalent to around €500 ($811) a month.

This would see her paying at a similar level to before the eviction.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and teal MP Allegra Spender have made a rare unified demand after the taxation office announced its plan to ban the use of credit cards for the payment of tax bills. Industry Minister Tim Ayres on Friday defended the move, blaming “profiteering” credit card companies for forcing the Australian Taxation Office’s hand amid growing anger on social media over Labor’s banning of card surcharges. Community Strong Australia MP Allegra Spender. Alex Ellinghausen The Reserve Bank of Australia on Thursday banned surcharges for Mastercard, Visa and eftpos networks, after a campaign from Labor the government said would save consumers $1.6 billion a year. As of October 1 merchants can no longer charge additional fees on checkout, which the Albanese government argues will save consumers money at the till. The move immediately prompted backlash from small business operators who say they will be forced to pass along charges to consumers in the upfront cost of goods and services. The RBA argues the transfer of charges to product pricing will inflate costs by around 0.1 per cent.

Advertisement

The tax office subsequently announced a plan to ban credit card transactions from November 30, saying in a statement: “As a government agency, the ATO has decided it would not be appropriate for the cost of credit card merchant fees to be transferred to the community,” an agency statement reads. The tax office said only 2.3 per cent of tax payments were made with credit cards in the 2024-25 financial year, and that 60 per cent of those charges were made by large organisations. “The credit card companies are charging too much, and that is a charge, ultimately, on the taxpayers because the ATO has to pay it. It’s a charge on Australian taxpayers. It’s not the right thing to do,” Ayres told News24 on Friday. “There are alternative ways of paying, and the ATO will work through that with their customers and their stakeholders.”

Advertisement

Spender on Friday called for the decision to be reversed, saying the ATO was acting hypocritically. “I’m hearing that all the time from people in my community who are small business [owners], and it’s particularly cash flow that is really hard to manage. So this is where I think the ATO should reverse this,” Spender told Nine’s Today show on Friday. Related Article Payments Cash discounts and refunds: Your card surcharge ban cheat sheet One Nation leader Pauline Hanson echoed Spender’s comments, saying the move was an “unintended consequence because [Labor] never think anything through”, as she joined calls from the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry for the decision’s reversal. “Businesses are expected to absorb these fees, while the ATO avoids them by withdrawing credit-card payments,” Hanson said.

Advertisement

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said the government was “insensitive”, as he sought to blame the decision on a lack of business experience from Labor MPs. “On the day that [Labor] impose these surcharges on small businesses, has decided that the ATO won’t take credit card payments because they don’t want the surcharges. I mean, seriously, you couldn’t make it up,” Taylor said. Several social media posts have gone viral accusing the government of inadvertently inflating the price of products, comically depicting business owners rolling merchant fees into the base cost of products. title: Why Broncos have ‘freakish’ rival to thank for their lethal spine
text:

SportNRLNRLW 2026 Why Broncos have ‘freakish’ rival to thank for their lethal spine Nick Wright October 2, 2026 — 2:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It took an impassioned plea from one of the NRLW’s leading superstars to entice Jada Ferguson back to rugby league, and on the cusp of a second premiership ring. The Brisbane Broncos hooker had been aged out of the game after under-12s, with her Toowoomba home town short of opportunities for girls beyond that. Broncos NRLW hooker Jada Ferguson. NRL Images She instead tried her hand at rugby sevens, before Queensland Maroons superstar Tarryn Aiken – who will line up against Ferguson for the Roosters in Sunday’s grand final – got in her ear. “Exactly,” Ferguson laughed, when put to her that if she helped inspire a Broncos triumph – having scored in last year’s decider – it would partly be by Aiken’s doing.

Advertisement

“I didn’t come back to rugby league until I was 18 when I moved down to the Gold Coast for university. We played touch together, and she said ‘come to league, come to league’,” Ferguson said. “I played with her at Tweed Seagulls, and then in my first year of league I made under-19s Origin and then got selected in the Broncos squad. She’s had a big impact on getting me over to rugby league, so it’s exciting to verse her and hopefully beat them. “She helps me to be confident in myself. She’s just a good mentor as well as a player, she does so well in the game and her eyes-up footy is unreal … she can make and break a game, she pulls off stuff that is pretty freakish.” Jada Ferguson and Tarryn Aiken playing for the Broncos together in 2021. NRL Images The pair have gone on to represent Queensland together, featuring in the 2025 series defeat. Ferguson’s touch football background has seeped into her rugby league career – finishing third for dummy-half runs in 2026 (52) and equal-first across the past three seasons (148) – and has cast her eye towards an Aiken reunion for Australia at this year’s World Cup.

Advertisement

When Ferguson arrived at Red Hill, Aiken was the marquee halfback of the Broncos – inspiring the club’s 2019 and 2020 premierships, the latter against her current Roosters outfit. Her fullback on that day was Tamika Upton, who will now chase her sixth NRLW premiership – a fourth for the Broncos, having won consecutive titles with the Newcastle Knights. Upton has been heralded the best player in the women’s rugby league space, with three Dally M Medals to show for it, but there is a strong case for Aiken to be considered in similar regard. Jada Ferguson, pictured being tackled by Olivia Kernick, has become a State of Origin star and Broncos premiership champion since being drawn back to rugby league. Getty Images “She’s an incredible player, I played a lot with her, and she’s probably the brains, but she’s also got the strike as well. She’s got the talent to get through the line, but she’s also one of the most talented at setting up other people around her, which is why they’re such a good team,” Upton said.

Advertisement

“It [our relationship] actually goes way back, I actually played a bit of touch football with Tarryn as well in our junior years, so I’ve known her for a very long time. It’s no coincidence she’s as good as she is; she works very hard, and she’s a very diligent trainer.” Brisbane edge forward and fellow Maroon Romy Teitzel added: “We’ve seen what Tarryn can do single-handedly for the Roosters, Jillaroos, and even alongside her in the Queensland arena. “She creates opportunities out of nothing, so she’ll be very dangerous for us, but she’s one player out of 17 who take the field for them this weekend. I also like my halfbacks as well, they can create some pretty cool opportunities.” Loading Having missed last year’s decider between the powerhouse clubs due to a knee injury, Aiken – who became the first player to be named in the Players’ Dream Team for a fifth time this year – is now out to ensure the career of retiring former teammate, Ali Brigginshaw, does not end on a high note.

Advertisement

She will enter the decider fresh off scoring the match-winning try against the Canberra Raiders to seal a preliminary final victory in an undefeated campaign, as Sydney seek to extract revenge from Brisbane’s 22-18 victory in 2025. “I’m just really proud to see her out there, I know she’s an enemy on Sunday, but she’s also been a teammate of mine, and to see her go down last year hurt. To see her back out there, we’d rather take on the best,” Brigginshaw said of the 27-year-old. “She’s a big game player and performing very highly. She directs that team, but they’ve got Tarryn Aiken, and we’ve got Jesse Southwell, so it’s the battle of the sevens out there, and that’s what I’m excited to see – two of the best going at it.” Stepping into Aiken’s old jersey this year has been arguably the brightest light in the NRLW, with Southwell relishing the challenge, before watching her childhood club – the Knights – end a 25-year wait between NRL grand final appearances.

Advertisement

“I, personally, didn’t think I’d be alive to see it, which is crazy. Newcastle would be buzzing right now, and it was buzzing when we made those grand finals,” Southwell said. The 21-year-old has gone on to hoist the silverware twice with Newcastle, guided New South Wales to State of Origin glory, represented Australia three times, and even won gold in rugby sevens at the 2022 Commonwealth Games. Jesse Southwell will seek to become a dual-club premiership-winner after guiding Newcastle to consecutive titles in 2021 and 2022. Getty But she concedes if not for Aiken, the trail may never have been blazed for her to attain such lofty heights, having taken elements of the 2024 Golden Boot winner’s running game and taken it further to lead the competition in line engagements (80). “I’ve definitely loved watching Tarryn. She’s an outstanding player, I think her stats speaks for itself, she’s one of the best players in rugby league,” Southwell said.

“You take things from different types of players, and Tarryn’s no exception. You want to be the best, and you’ve got to watch the best, so I’m learning a lot of different things from different players, and she’s definitely one of them.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. title: ANZ drops KPMG as auditor after almost 60 years
text:
ANZ has dropped KPMG after almost 60 years of the firm holding the $29.3 million contract to audit the bank’s accounts, in a fresh blow to the consulting firm that continues to contend with the fallout from a damaging whistleblower scandal.

An anonymous KPMG whistleblower warned the firm of a raft of serious allegations, including that senior partners had misused confidential information to win work, but was given short shrift until Senator Deborah O’Neill went public with the allegations in March.

ANZ has ditched KPMG as its auditors after they worked together since 1969. Bloomberg

That has led to companies including Macquarie Bank ditching KPMG as their auditors in a series of repercussions that escalated on Friday when ANZ announced its board had also decided to open up its contract for tender.

“ANZ’s external audit service has been provided by KPMG since 1969,” a spokesman said. He attributed the bank’s decision to the length of time KPMG had worked with the bank, and did not mention the whistleblower scandal that has led to numerous senior staff leaving and mass layoffs.

Connor Watson is officially out of Sunday’s NRL grand final after failing to overcome a concussion. The Sydney Roosters confirmed on Friday that Watson would be unable to play against the Knights, which would have doubled as his farewell game from the club before moving on to St George Illawarra. Loading Roosters coach Trent Robinson is now expected to call on Benaiah Ioelu, a Samoan international who has played just five NRL games this season, to replace Watson. Watson underwent testing with a specialist on Thursday morning, and was due to have further examinations that night, in the hope of being cleared.

Advertisement

The representative utility had only been on the field for one minute on Friday against the Dolphins when he suffered the concussion. Watson was initially ruled to have displayed category-two symptoms, but that was later upgraded to category one. That meant he was automatically forced to stand down from training and playing for 11 days under the NRL’s concussion protocols, essentially ending his grand final dream. Connor Watson will know by Friday if he is free to play in the grand final. Getty Images The Roosters monitored Watson’s condition on Saturday and in the days that followed, and had been expected to ask the NRL to review the category-one grading in the hope it would be reclassified as a category two, which removes the mandatory 11-day enforced rest. One of the country’s top neurologists, Mark Parsons, stressed the risks involved in rushing Watson back, telling this masthead at the start of the week: “I’d be very surprised if an independent neurologist would clear him.”

Advertisement

Several sources with knowledge of the situation not authorised to speak publicly said the NRL were worried about Watson suffering a second head knock on Sunday, even if he had been cleared. It is a shattering way for Watson to miss a decider considering his awful run with injuries over the years. Connor Watson gets knocked out on Friday night. Channel Nine Ioelu, 22, is the logical choice to be the back-up dummy half on the bench. “If he [Watson] is out, I’ve got other players who will step in who have played many games and are really clear on their roles,” Robinson said on Thursday.

“Connor, we want him to play, he deserves to play. Whether he’s fit to play will get decided by someone else, then we’ll adapt. “I don’t think it would take too much to work our what plan B is. We have some really good hookers. Benaiah Ioelu has played some really good footy for us this year. He brings a lot of energy, and he’ll come into consideration.” James Tedesco leads the Roosters out at Thursday’s Fan Fest in Martin Place. The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.
